summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. 1966 and March 31st, 1967 in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The respondent assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Wealth Tax officer rejected the contention and deleted the additions of Rs 1, 50,000 representing accrued interest. In doing so, the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: Under section 3 of the Wealth tax Act wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee On the valuation date, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation day. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset.

The Inquiry Officer framed charges against the respond ent in the following terms: "That the said Shri Parma Nand, while working as Time Keeper, in time Keeping Sub Division of Beasati Sutle ngi during the month of May 1969 failed to maintain absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as mu ch he falsely marked the attendance of Shri Ashok Kumar, Token No. 59 T with the sign a tures of the issuing officer was also prepared by the r e spondent although it was not his duty to prepare the ident i ty card. The said fictitious identity card was used by o ne Suraj Singh, cleaner T. No. 210 K of Beggi Tunnelling Divi sion for the purpose of withdrawing the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month May 1969 even though Ash ok Kumar was not working in that Division. A bogus identi ty card in the name o f Ashok Kumar R/o. 59, T with a sign tures issued by the respondent although it is not his ly duty to preparing the iti ty card pertaining to 'T ' Token of Central Survey Division Sundernagar for the period May 1969 and entered the names of Ashok kuma r. While Suraj Singh by impersonation was receiving the pay o f he was recognised by the Cashier since he kn ew him personally. There then started an enquiry followed by departmental proceedings against three persons includ ing the respondent herein. The Personnel Officer of the 23 BSL Project was appointed as Inquiry Officer. The inquiry officer framed charge against the respondent in the follow terms: (i) That the said Sri Parma n Nand, While working as time Keeper in Time Keeping Sub division of Bea Sutle j Li nk Project, Sundarnagar during the period of May1969 failed to maintaining absolute integrity & devotion to duties in as Mu ch he h falsely marked attendance of Mr Ashok Kumar; (ii) That he ma ste r minded and prepared the pay roll pertaining to T 'Token of central Survey Division, Sunder Nagar for the months of May, 1969 failed maintain absolute ability and devotion t he to duty In as mu sh as he falsely marking the attendance in the p ay roll of May 4969; (iii) That on account of the aforesaid misconduct, it cannot be termed th at that the finding returned by the Inquiry Officer is without a ny evidence. The Tribunal held that the respondent was guilty of entering the name in the pay Roll for May 1969, and so far as other three colleagues in whose cases only future increments were stopped, the maxi mum being for three years in respect of Shri Sain Ditt a, Clerk. An appreciation of the evidence as done in the preceding pages, would sh ow that the applicant had entered the said name with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay. The Tribun al also held that he was guilty and awarded a lesser penalty on the ground that it is disproportionate to the proved misdemeanour of the charge proved against him and is in stark contrast to the punishment awarded to his other three co n ties in whose case, only future increment were stopped. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Tribunal.

The appellants, the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that he was not in possession of the suit property and therefore a suit was barred by res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal, the High Court held that the suit was not barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. That suit was for a declaration that the plaintiff was a lessee and for an injunction restraining the defendants therefrom from dispossess ing him from his property known to 'Panmar Oateral do. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff had not been dispossessed,in accordance with law, the defen dants who were mere trespassers were liable to be evicted. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that defendant No 1 was a trespasser in the property and was liable to he evicted therefrom; that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by section 9 of the Act, defendant No 2 was, therefore, entitled to let out the property to defendant Nos. 1 and hence the latter was in lawful possession thereof till his possession came to be disturbed sometime in June, 1968; that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable; that since he was a tenant in respect of the demised property apprehended his forcible dispossession therefrom; and that even if the plaintiff 's lease was terminated as stipulated by section 18 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939, defendant 2 was therefore entitled to become a deemed purchaser of the said suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The High court was wrong in holding that the subject matter of the second Suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed the second plaintiff suit was clearly barred by Order 2 rule 2(2) of Code of civil Procedure.

The petitioners are working as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they have sought enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". The petitioners, who were carpenterers 1 and 2th grade employed in the Wood working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh state Handicrafts Corpora tion (the Corpo ration) contended that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: The principle of "equal Pay for equal Work" has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore not impermissible to provide two different pay scales in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [667B] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. (i) The principle that equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of that right cannot be enforced invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It follows naturally that equal Pay for unequal Work will be one concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitu tion. But it follows naturally, that equal wages for equal pay will be an negation of this right. Thus the law relating to equal pay in the light of all the previous decisions of this Court. [668C D] (ii) The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable to their counterparts in Government service. Secondly, it may be noted that the petitioners are carpentors; better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. The two jobs by the mere nomen clature or by the volume of work performed cannot be rated as equal. It was not just a comparison of physical activity. It requires the consideration of various dimensions of the job. The accuracy required by the job and the dexterity it entails may differ from job to job. It cannot be evaluated by the Mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. [669F H] (iii) The Court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. Meva Ram Kanojia vs All India Institute of Medical Sciences, ; ; , relied on.

The accused were charged with the offence of murder and for the murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to them. The Sessions Judge found that the evidence against the accused was not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted him. He convicted and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for the offence under section 304 Part II, Part 11, Part II of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed his appeal on the ground that the conviction of one of the accused alone was unsustainable in law having regard to the requirement of section 120A I. P.C., and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Court and also the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No. 4 which was framed only against accused 1, 6 and 7. It was contended on behalf of the State that the judgment of the High court confirming his conviction and sentence awarded to him by the trial court under section302 read with Section 34 I.p.C could be sustained. Allowing the appeal of accused 5 and acquitting him, this Court, HELD: (1) The retracted judicial confession of accused 1 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact of that accused 6 who had been tried along with accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Courts of charge No 4 framed under Section 302 readwith section 120 B I.I.P.,C. [785F] (2) The evidence regarding the presence of accused 7 and the approver P.W. 1 near about the scene of offence before and after the murder, of Malan was amply corroborated by other evidence, namely, recovery of the blood stained razor blade, article 54 and the medical evidence of Dr. Suresh (P.W 31) who had conducted autopsy on the body of Malin at 4.15 p.m. on 2.1.1976. The doctor found 9 incised wounds on various parts of the body including the right side of the vagina outside in the middle and a small incised injury on the lower end of the femoral just at the mouth and he was of the opinion that all the 11 injuries were antemortem injuries which might have been caused by sharp cutting weapons, that it is possible that injuries 5 to 7 found on the forehead and right side would collectively be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [781F] Topandas vs State of Bombay, ; , referred to.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) in favour of her husband Sadagopalachar. According to the plaint under the will respondent I was entitled only to a life interest in items 1 and 2 and that on her death the said items would vest in respondents 2 to 4 and respondent 5 respectively. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against respondent I in respect of items 3, 4 and 5 and a declaration that respondent I had only a life estate interest in item No. 2 was not genuine or valid and that at the material time Lakshmma was not in sound disposing state of mind. The trial court held that the will was genuine and valid to the extent of the share belonging to the testatrix. On appeal, the High Court held that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that it was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the will and put her signature on it when she was in a sound disposing and disposing state. Held, further, that the High court was right in holding that the appellant had not established that the testator fully understood or the contents thereof and put his signature on the instrument intending that the recitals and dispositions in the will should be her recitals and disposition. The onus of proving the execution of the document lies in every case upon the party propounding a will and he must satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument so propounded is the last will of a free and capable testator 's mind and his signature as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour.

The appellants, who were engaged in the manufacture of Arcbons, manufactured by them, were assessed to sales tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The High Court held that the goods under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No., 4 in the 1th schedule of the Act. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ. [564B C] (2) The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that 'the main use of the arc carbons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as "cinema arc carboons" in the market. [565E F] (3) The word 'accessories ' is used In the schedule of making the entry in each case. The best guide to their intentions is the language actually employed by them.

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by Section 15 of the (67 of 1957) and the validity thereof. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the state Government had to be used only for minerals development and could not be used for any other purpose. According to them the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy in question is in the nature of a tax and it was not in the character of a fee which could be used by only for specific purposes. Any tax realised by the Govern ment forms part of consolidated fund or of the state and the said tax can be used in any other manner sanctioned by law. [403B C] 2. The fact that in the other States the royalty is fixed at Re. 1 per metric tonne of Black Trap and Hard Murrum and Rs.7 levied in the notification is not by itself sufficient to hold that Rs. 7 per metric tonnes was unreasonably high rate of royalty. In Trivedi 's case this Court had upheld the levy of Rs.4 per metric litre which had been fixed in 1981 and in 1985 it was increased to Rs.6,000 per metric ton. [414C D] 3. The question whether a valid classification of persons and things for 414 purposes of imposing any obligation on them would not be violative of Article 14 provided the classification is a reasonable one. It is well settled that a classification to be valid has to satisfy two conditions: (1) that there is an intelligible differentia between those who are included in the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who arc placed outside the said rule; and (2) that the object to be achieved by the rule or law in question.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was "hereditary" within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 1 of 1925. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the Temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the. meaning of s 6( 9) of Act 19 of 1951. HELD: (i) The term "succession" in section 6 (9) means that the trustee has a beneficial interest of some sort or not. [445 B] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , referred to. (ii)The word "sucaccession ' is defined as follows: "the revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution". The fact of the transmission of the rights, estate obligations and charges of a deceased person to his heir or heirs does not rest upon independent title. [427 C] State Of Madras vs B. Ramakrishna, A.I.R. 1954 S.C.

The appellant was the village Munsif (Headman) of a village. On April 26, 1971 at about 10 P.M. he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 p.m. He saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) running ahead of accused Karunakaran Padayachi running eastwards from the place where he was sitting and who fell down on the northern side of the sluice. When he went near him he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more as punctured and the remaining one as a vertical incised wound. These were on the left side of his leg, on the right side of epigastrium, on his left arm, on an upper arm, left side, on a mid axillary line, on which the right hand side of that epighatrium was running after stabbing him with knife. The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) there had been a history of bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased Viswanatham t on the other; (ii) there was no evidence against him; (iii) there could be no infirmity in convicting the appellant; (iv) there were no eye witnesses who arrived at the place of occurrence, and (v) there is a mention about a pool of blood only where the dead body was found at No. 1 in the first information report. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court was not right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the contents of the FIR. On the other hand it has r shown that his version in the FIR stood contradicted by the testimony in court on a very material point. [711B] (2) There is a reference about a Pool of blood even where the deceased body was seen at No 1 in court for the purpose of corroborating PW 4. If the statement of PW 4 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the scene of occurrence already when he arrived. It is also conceivable that those persons who arrived would not ask PW 4, who arrived there at the places a little later, for information with regard to the assailants.

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of work done up to the death Of Amarchand the realisation were to be divided amongst the respondents and the real collections were to he divided amongst all the respondents. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the five assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55 the Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under section 34 could validly be served only for the assessment years 1951 52 and 1952 53. On appeal by the respondents the Tribunal held that in view of section 24B(1) of the Act the amounts were not taxable and that the section had no application to the case. Held, that on a correct interpretation of section24B the amounts which were received by the heirs and legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24 B(1), but in that case also the amount was received by him before his death and that received by his heirs and Legal representatives after their death but in the previous year became assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment year. The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 23B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the earlier year. In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, , referred to.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All of them were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969, leaders of political parties in the Legislature of the State appeared to have met and reached the decision that to Implement what are called Telengana Safeguards ', the following measures should be taken : "All non domicile persons who have been appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra pra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 for domiciles of Telengna region will be immediately relieved from service. The posts so rendered vacant will be filled by qualified candidates possessing domicile qualifications and in cases where such candidates are not available the posts shall be left unfilled till qualified domicile candidates become available action on the above lines will be taken immediately. All non domicile employees so relieved shall be provided employment in the Andhra region without break in service and by creating supernumerary posts, if necessary. " The Government of Andhra Pradesh then passed an order (G.O.Ms. 36, G.A. (SR) Department on January 21, 1969 relieving all non domicile person appointed on or after November 1, 1956 to certain categories of posts reserved for domicics of Telangana region under the State Public Employment Act, 1957. The petitioners challenged the Act and the Rules and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. Their case was that article 16(3) under which the Act, and the rules purport to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to make, a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act, 1898. The prosecution case was that when the house in which the appellant lives along with his father Diwan Singh, a retired Police Head Constable was searched by the C.I.D. Inspector, S.N. Singh, along with Masood Murtaza, Sub Inspector of Police, Bulandshahr on May 12, 1956 in connection with a case against Messrs Greenwood Publicity, they accidentally discovered a large number of letters and postcards and also the five registered letters in question. At the time of search the appellant who happens to be a trade union official was not in Bulandshahr but was away on leave at Delhi in connection With a postal conference. The articles were found in an almirah and the key of which was produced by the appellant 's father was produced before him. The appellant ' defence in all these cases was that there were two factions in the Bulandshahr post office and that these articles were planted by the opposite party. According to him neither the house nor the almirah from which the articles were said to have been seized was in his exclusive possession. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the appellant. The mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees.

The appellants were alleged to have been abused and were being laboured and his property worth Rs. 40/ damaged. The Magistrate, after recording evidence, passed an order directing the accused to postpone proceedings pending the receipt of the stay order. On December 23, 1963, the Sarpanch, filed an application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947, to transfer the proceedings on the ground that the complainant and the members of the Bench, Opposite Parties Nos. 2 to 5 disobeyed the order of the High Court and disposed of the case on 25 12 63. The appellants contended that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayats when no proceeding was pending before him. Held: (i) In matters those who assert that a person had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying the order. The question then arises whether the Sarpanch and the Pan chas had knowledgeof the existence of the said order of High Court dated December 20, 1963. (ii) In such matters those which assert that the person had know of the existence must prove the fact beyond doubt. (iii) Where there is no doubt, that the benefit should be given in the case of a person who bona fide came to the conclu sion on the basis of the material before him, that source of the information isnot authentic he can be held liable for contempt of courts for disobey ing the order and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of Courts. (iv) In cases where a person bonafide comes to this conclusion on material placed on him that source the source from which information is information is no authentic he could be held to guilty of Contempt of Court.

The appellant was charged with the murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed in village Bhadurpur Ghar, with a sword at about mid night on the night between June 14, 1960. The trial court convicted him under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced him to death. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the extra judicial confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh found ample support from the facts that the appellant did purchase a sword day before the incident and deposited it stained with human blood at the Police Station on the morning of the murder are sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder had committed the murder. The extra judicial confessions are not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person, who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June. Both on account of the temperature and on account Of the culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant 's bathing in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to be improbable. It is not a matter of surprise that he wakes up and proceeds to the spot from where the splashing sound which is supposed to be due to the wading of the neel gais came. The Canal runs beside Ujagar Singh 's field. Ujagar Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High Court, since if it was held that the appellants were not vigilant in moving before the High court, it would become unnecessary to go into the other questions raised before this Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High 'Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [495E F] 1.2 The power under Article 136 of the constitution to issue a writ is ordinarily discretionary and the High courts are not justified in entertaining the petition on account or on the inordinate delayed delay involved in the presentation of the writ petition. [596F G] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioners had filed a claim to include his name in the electoral Roll on October 19, 1978 and that was rejected by the Deputy Collector without following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. The claim of petitioner No. 5 was rejected as no evidence in support of his claim was produced before the Deputy Commissioner. It was also not open to them to file a writ petition immediately after the publication of such notice questioning its legality. None of the above courses was adopted by the petitioners. Persons whose claims were rejected could have filed an appeal under Rule S before the Collector. No such appeal was presented. The final electoral roll was published on November 16, 1978. It is notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978, and the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 31, 1978 at the request of the counsel for the petitioners.[596A B] 2:2 In the course of the discussion with the press reporters on that day, the Minister had stated that he had directed the Commissioner, Raipur Division, Raipur, to entertain their claim for inclusion in the Electoral Roll and he refused to receive their applications. It could not place any reliance on the news item for the purposes of concluding that the Collector, Raipur had been informed about the defect of the defects in the notices issued under rule 4(i) of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation (Amendment) Rules, 1978 by October 21, 1978.[597C D] 2 :3 The period prescribed for preferring claims and objections under Rule 5(3) was 30 days. It would be open to all persons who were interested in preferring claims or objections to file them within a period of 20 days.

The respondent company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section. The Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A.I.R. 1970 Orissa 78 held that if no balance sheet was laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balance sheets and profit loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , and (2) the principles accepted by the Supreme Court in the State of Madras vs Bandhin Ram Bhandarani & Anr. ; referred to. HELD : (i) Under section 134 of the Companies Act 1913, the laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid should be filed before the Registrar. The intention is made further clear by the provision under sub s.(2) of section 133 of the Old Companies Act or sub section(1), of section 221 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. [415 F] (ii) Under Section 134 of Companies the laying off a balance sheets or profit & loss account after the expiry of 21 days from the date of the first or only ordinary general meeting in the year is made obligatory. The failure to comply with section 131 is made punishable under section 135(4). [416 A B] (iii) The provisions of sections 134 and 132 of the are not complied with. [416 C] (iv) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit & Loss account or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, have been laid before the company at the general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 D] (v) The liability of sending three copies of the balancesheet and profit or loss account or income and the expenditure account, as the ease may be arises only after they have been provided before the general body meeting of the Company at a general meetings under section 131 and that where in a case there is no such placing of the remaining balance sheet before the Company, three copies thereafter shall be sent to the Registrar even without the necessity of their being laid before it. [420 E] (vi) The requirement of section 132 cannot be complied with because the provisions are not mandatory. The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum, and were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5(1) of the Act, under which it was sent to that court for trial was uncon vtitutional and void under article 13 (2)as it denied to him the equal protection of laws enjoined by article 14. Held, that the classification must not be arbitrary but must be rational, that is to say, it must not only be based on some quali fications or characteristics which are to be found in all the persons grouped together and not in others who are left out but those qualities or characteristics must have a reasonable relation to the object of the legislation. The classification must be reasonable and must be based upon some intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons from others left out, and that differentia must be such as to exclude persons from the class of persons grouped along and not others who were left out. Held further, that in judging whether this argument applies to a case it must be borne in mind that although the classification, if any, is illusive or evasive, but no question of intention can arise when discrimination follows or arises on the express terms of the law itself. The State Government in the present case had acted under that part of the section which authorised it to direct " cases" to be tried by a Special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the speedier trial of certain offences, and this was not a good enough classification.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The dispute related to fixation of wages including minimum wages and this was covered by items Nos. 1, 3, 4, 22 and 26 in the Schedule attached to the order of reference. The Tribunal gave its award on all thirty items. The Special Leave in this Court was sought and granted in respect of two matters covering some of these items. In the course of arguments before this Court it was contended that (1) the Tribunal committed an error at this stage in merely holding that the facts found by it justified a revision and in not proceeding to fix minimum wages on the basis of the other industries in the region, is fully justified; (2) even in adopting the latter course, the Tribunal committing an error inasmuch as, in making the calculation, the tribunal only tried to neutralise about 36 per cent of the cost of living the basis Of the rise in Price Index instead of permitting neutralisation to the extent of at least 90%, which could have been done when fixing the minimum wages for the owest class of workmen. HELD : (1)(a) The Tribunal committed no error in arriving at this decision and, consequently, the total minimum wage fixed by it must also be deemed to have the same break up. [669 C] French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs Its Workmen ; , followed. (b) In fixing the Minimum Wages, the wages payable in the paper industry in other parts of the country should also be kept in view. The principle laid down by this Court in French Motor car Co. case is not rigid and it is not necessary that the minimum wage. in the Company must be fixed at the average level of 'wages in the other comparable industries in that region. [670 D] (c) In determining the minimum Wages, one point has to be taken into account when applying the principle of fixing the maximum wage primarily on the ground of comparison between different industries in a particular region, and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into consideration. The concept of minimum wage does take in the factor of the prevailing cost of essen (1 ) ; , , , and in any case is that the dearness allowances form a part of the consolidated wage fixed, there should be such linking so as to bring in continuous variation of the wage depending on the variation in the Price Index. [671 E F] French Car Co. vs The Workmen, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 673, referred to. (2)(a). In fixing minimum wages, one question has to consider is whether the Tribunal had acted improperly or not and that the Tribunal was justified in taking into account the entire wage packet to be received by each workman and, in the opinion of the Tribunal, it would be appropriate under the circumstances of the case to fix the minimum minimum wage in the company on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs.95 which is the average minimum wage payable by those industries (1)[1963] Suppl. 673 and (b).

The appellant was carrying on a business in the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The partnership deed provided that the business of the firm shall be carried on by a person different from those who carried it on on April 1, 1939. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also the Tribunal held that the partnership deed was valid and that the income tax authorities were right in rejecting the claim. In reference the High Court held that on the facts and circumstances of the case the appellant firm was not liable to pay tax under section 24(4). The present appeals are from the judgment of the High court. Held, that the High Courts were right when they decided against the appellant. The business which had been subjected to tax in respect of which alone the benefit of section 25 (3) can be obtained. It is only if there was a discontinuance of the business before 1948 or a succession not amounting to a mere change in the constitution of the partnership between 1939 and 1948 that the appellants could be denied the benefit under section 26(2). The fact that he was not taken on in the original business also shows that the original firm business in respect Of which alone, the benefit was claimed continued uninterrupted. The appellant 's suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses, a land, two shops avoidables on the basis that these properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The plaintiff claimed a 7 /24th shares in the joint Hindu family properties. The trial court rejected the defendant 's case that the suit properties belonged only to the Joint Family, that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 1/4th share. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she was entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband interest upon his death. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the suit property belonged to a joint family, that the partition had taken place during her lifetime; (2) the plaintiff 's claim based as it was on the provisions of section 6, was essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest which her husband had at the time of his death in the coparcenary property. HELD : (1)(a) The High Court has based itself on the judgment in Rangubai Lalji vs Laxman Lalji, ; and Commissioner of Income tax, Delhi vs section Teja Singh, A.I.R. 1975 (Bombay) 257, referred to. (b) In overlooking that 1/3rd share, one unwittingly permits one 's imagination to boggle under the oppression of the reality that there is in fact no partition between the plaintiff and his sons. Whether a partition had actually taken place between the deceased and his coparceners immediately before his death, the point of time of the partition being the one immediately before the death of the person in whose property the heirs claim a share. [766 H] (c) The assumption that 1 /4th shares were to be ascertained on the reasoning that they bad separated from one another and had received a share In the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Hindu Succession Act, the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is capable of being disposed of by a will or other testamentary disposition. [765 C] (2)(a). The assumption which the statute requires to be made that a partition has in fact taken place must permeate the entire process of ascertainment of the ultimate share of the heirs, through all its stages. To make the assumption at the initial stage for the limited purpose of ascertaining the share of heirs is truly to permit one 'S imagination to fallgle under section 6(1)(b). [767 D] (b). The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in interest which the deceased had in the coparcener coparcenary property at the relevant time of their death, in addition to the share in which he or she received or must be deemed to have received in the notional partition.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were amended by the Life Insurance Corpora tion (Amendment) Act, 1981 with effect from 20th June, 1979. The said amendment was replaced by a new sub regulation which was notified on September 3, 1966. The first proviso to this sub section provided that notwithstanding anything contained in sub section (1) of section 11 or in any contract of service, the Central Government might for the purposes of rationalising the pay scales of employees of insurers whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it or for the pur pose of reducing the remu neration payable to those employees in cases where in the interest of the Corporation and its policyholders a reduction in the remuneration payable to such employees in case where in t he interest of such Corpora tation and the other terms and conditions of service applicable, to employees or any class of them was called for, the central Government may, notwith standing anything contained In sub section(1) or in the , or in a contract of serv ice, the State Government might, by order, direct such employee to retire on completion of 55 years of age or at any time thereafter, if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. The second proviso to that sub section empowered the appointing authority to extend at its discretion the service of any employee of the Corpo ration belonging to Class I or class II categories appointed to the service on or after 1st September 1956 for one year at a time upto 60 years ofage. The amendment made by the new sub clause (2) of that sub clause empowered the appointment authority to reduce at its pleasure the service and to make such employee liable to retire from service on completion thereof of 55 year of age, but the competent authority may, if it is of the opinion that it was in the interests of the Corpora ny to do so, direct the employee to be retired on completion Of 50 years of service or at a place thereafter, on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The proviso further provided that where the Central Govern ment is satisfied that for the purpose of securing uniformity in the scales of remuneration a reduction and the conditions of serv ices applicable to employees of the insurers whose regulated business had not been transferred ted to and vest in it, it is necessary so to do, or that, in the public interest, the Corporation may, by an order, extend his service for one month at atime upto 60 year of 58 years. The respondent who was employed as a Class I employee in the appellant Corporation was compulsorily retired from service under the provisions of the Life Corpora ly Act on attaining the age of superannuation. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2) and the amendment made to Regulation 19 by the Central Legislature. The High Court held that the employees of tho Corpo tion belonging to class I and Class II who had entered service of the appellant corporation after 1.9.1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond the age Of 58 years, and directed the Corporation to continue him in its service till he completed the ageof 60 years subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the respondent that since he had the right to continue to remain in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age oth 60 years as a class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendments made in section 11(2), the age for retirement in his case could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a Class II post.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial als of a Judge. The letter was addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana, the Prime Minister of India, Chief Justice and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab & Haryana High Courts. The appellants filed contempt petitions in the High Court against the judgment and order of the Full Bench of the High court. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of the Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. Each of them affirmed an affidavit in this pattern. The deponent tendered his apology to this Hon ' Court for the same and prayed for its acceptance. The Full Bench also referred to paragraph 9 of the affidavit where the deponents said that "if in view of this Honble Court,the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself". The High 'Court did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of Court. It was also necessary to state here that if any Judge address es on political problems or controversies the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The reason is obvious. It is no part of the duty of a judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a Judges to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court would take any steps against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. The reasons are obvious. The Court was of the view that the matter did not constitute any contempt. The judgment is set aside and the contempt proceedings are dropped.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. The respondent was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The estate was then settled to the British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj Chet Singh to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhithala in perpetuity to Babu Au Ram Hat Narain Singh anal his heirs in perpetuity. The quantum of this pension was calculated on the basis of 1/4th of the revenue of the Jagir. By this arrangement the revenue or land collections of Jagir became payable by the Zamindars direct to the Government and by the grant of the pension, Babu Hat Narain singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and became entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8 was dated 7th July 1837 and from H. Elliot Esqr., the Secretary to Lt. Government, NWP. Allahabad, to J. Thompson Esq, Offg. Secretary to the Board of Revenue N.W.P. High Court held that the amount which had been received by the successors of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year and was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The source of the income was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income. Held, that the allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income under section 4 (3)(ix) of Income tax.

The appellant 's predecessor in interest, granted a lease of 96 bighas out of his 400 bighas to one D. M. Mathews, the predecessor in title of the appellant, who was the predecessor of the respondents, on October 11, 1901, and on November 23, 1900, it appears that Samanta bad surrendered his rights under the previous lease in favour of the Raja and taken a fresh lease of the same plot of 96 acres to one Walji Khetan representing the appellant. The appellants ' case was that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines on August 18, 1941, the appellants made an inquiry and came to know that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. On these allegations they asked for the following reliefs: (a) That the intermediate boundary line between the two leaseholds i.e., between the appellant ' and the respondents ' predecessor in interests clearly demarcates the boundary line; (b)That the area encroached upon by the appellants be ascertained and fixed; (c)That a permanent injunction be issued against the defendants restraining them from encroaching upon the plaintiffs coal land and cutting and removing coal therefrom. The trial court held that article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that they had knowledge of the encroachment only in 1941. On appeal, the High Court accepted all the findings of the courts below and dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The finding of the Courts below was vitiated by an error of law by the burden of proof having been wrongly thrown on the appellant; (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove the knowledge of his father wag within three years of the suit; (iii) The burden of proving that he first learnt within three year of the date of the filing of the plaint was certainly on the respondents. Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, A.I.R. , Rangnekar, J., formulated the legal position thus: "The onus is on the plaintiff to prove in the former sense is certainly on his defendants. But the question is whether they have adduced evidence which had the effect of shifting the burden Of proof to the appellant." (iv) The Commissioner appointed by the Court tested the position of the six trijunction pillars shown in the map of lease dated November 23 1900, and found that two of the trijram pillars were in their correct positions. On the basis of these two trijayam pillars, the Commissioner relaid, by the process of superimposition, the northern boundary line of the leasehold property, The point A in the maps accepted by the High court was that the demarcation of the lease hold was incorrect and that two or four of the Trijunction pillar pillars were not in their proper positions.

The appellant, a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On August 9, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18(A). In appeal by special leave: Held: (i) The employer could defend the act under r., 18(c) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under that rule. (ii) Even in a case of this kind the requirement of bona fides is essential and if the terminaton of service is a colourable exercise, of the powers or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. (iii) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(i). But the Tribunal has pointed out in the circumstances that if the employer wanted to take action for misconduct and then suddenly dropped the departmental proceedings which were intended to be held and decided to discharge the employee under r .18(a), it was clearly a colourable exercised exercise of power and was therefore not bona fide or was a result Of victimisation or victimisation or fair labour practice.

The appellants were the owners of a cinema theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and G, the receivers granted to the latter on certain conditions and conditions. "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad against Raval and Ejabwala and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960 to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 31, 1960, the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and C were bound and liable to allow Filmistan to exercise its "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval & Fara Qui were bound to execute and register" an agreement in writing incorporating the said agreement with the variation as to rental. Pursuant to this agreement, a fresh agreement was executed on December 1 1960. On September 1, 1963, Filmisten filed suit No 1465 of 1963 in the court of Small Cause at Ahmedabad inter alia for a declaration of that as sub lessee or as lessee under law it was not entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the cinema theatre and to exhibit cinematograph films and to hold "entertainment performances" etc. in the premises, and also against Baldevdas Shivlal who claimed to be the owner of the Theatre. The suit was based on the claim by Filmiston as lessees or sub lessees of the Cinema theatre and was exclusively triable by the Court. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The order passed by the High court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [439 F] (2) A consent decree, accord ing to the decisions of this Court does not operate as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as a res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 E] (3) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. 442 This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, A.I.R. , that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and it includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to the extent to which the court, viz., the trial court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question or decide that question over again to the effect that question was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1. 1960, to be reopened, it is proposing to exercise the jurisdiction which is not vested in it by law. [442 F G] (4) The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue of res judicata or any other issue.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) An order of acquittal can be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial or compelling reasons". [367B] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. (2) The discrepancies in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The Sessions Judge allowed himself to be assailed by airy and fanciful doubts. [367E F] San wat Singh vs State Of Rajasthan, ; , followed. (3) An injury of the nature received by the deceased could have been caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [368B] (4) The injuries were inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. The location of the injury was 6 cms. below the arm pit on the left side. According to the accused, the deceased received the injury when she placed herself between P. W. 1 and himself. It was obvious that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill the deceased. It could not be said that he had any deep motives to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. [369E F; 370A] Sanchal Singh & Anr. vs The State of Rajasthan, A.I.R. 1971 S.C.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted for having committed an offence under section 5(1) (c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court dismissed his appeal and confirmed the conviction. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the President is given the power to appoint Judges of the High Court as well as of the Chief Justice of India by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of a Supreme Court and of the high Court, in the States as he may deem necessary for that purpose and in case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Jus tice, the President appoints a Judge by warrant and seal upon the Chief Justices of India, the Governor of the State and in a case of appoint ment of a judge other than Chief Justice or Chief Justice. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a High Court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in article 2 18 read with Article 124(4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution for removal of the Judge. [822E] 1.2 In the case of such public servants whenever sanction to prosecute is sought under section 6 of the Act, the competent authority can form the requisite opinion on the basis of the available material including the service record of the public servant to come to the conclusion whether the offence under clause (e) of sub section (1) of Section 5 of the said Act, is made out prima facie. [889B] 1:3 The President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the, Supreme Court or of the 'High Court from his office though the Presi dent appoints the Judge by warrants under his hands and seal and similarly even after passing of an address by both Houses of Parliament in the manner provided in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), placed before the President a Judge cannot be removed from his Office unless and order to that effect is passed by the President. The President, therefore, being the authority competent to appoint and remove a judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 122, clauses 4 and 5 of Article124 read with article 218, it is not so for him to contend that sanction thereunder can be obtained for the prosecution of a person holding such an office.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of the High Court on the ground that he did not belong to a Scheduled caste and that it was, therefore, not open to him at the trial to contend, as he appeared to have done. Held, that the appeal must fail. The appellant was not a member in a Scheduled Castes specified in item 40 of the President 's Order. To decide whether the respondent had established that the appellant belonged to a smaller caste group within the Sunri caste, no question of Sahas being a distinct class independent of Sunris,could arise. The finding that Sahas were a wholly independent caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence cannot alter the natural interpretation of the words in the order. For the same reason, the High court held that the Sahas formed a distinct caste wholly outside the Suniti caste and they had been specifically excluded in item40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin. The result then was that the respondent was a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste. The Tribunal came to its conclusion that it had not, therefore. been prov ed in this case that the appel lant belonged to the Saha group within that the Sunmi caste. Held further, that on the evidence led in the case as they appeared to be imperfect.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was alleged that the appellant demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 which was later on reduced to Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The appellant 's wife denied any aiding and abetting her husband in the commission of the two offences. The Presidency Magistrate convicted him under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 and sentenced him to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30, 000. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court summarily dismissed the appeal on the ground that what was received by the appel lant was by way of pugree. As section 18(1) of that Act was not applicable he convicted him thereunder under section19(2). Held: (i) The word "relinquishment" does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the 5534 relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. The section in question, it should be further noted that an assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It is the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an ac quired offence. Then follows section 19 which speaks of the relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises by a tenants. If, by the expression, an assignment such as we have in the present case was meant, appropriate words could have been used, such as the transfer by a lessee of his interest, which is made unlawful under section 15. Section 18(2), does not speak of relinquishment or giving up possession,in general terms. The words are "the relinquishment of" of his rights of any posi tion. The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of his right as such. Whether abandonment of a ' tenancy would come within the meaning of relinquishment is a question that does not arise in this appeal because in the face of Exhibit D, there was no abandonment in the sense that the tenant disappeared from the scene altogether saying nothing and making no arrange ments about his interest and possession under the lease.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership concern and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Union. The company had its office at Bombay. It functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and did not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consisted of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306 were members of the appellant 's Tata Engineering Employees Union. They served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was urged that the Efficiency Bar as a feature of the wages scale should be removed, and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the Appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the workmen that having regard to the financial capacity of the company the Tribunal erred in making the wage scale retrospective and in any event, in ranging the retrospectivity back to 1st January 1976; that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsman and Rs. 100/ to every workman in tho case of other categories, a result wholly unwarranted, it is said by the intent of the original award and, therefore, falling beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal; that there was fierce competition also, it had been asserted from other similar organisations; that even when considering the range of permissible retrospectivity the Tribunal stated in the award: "In view of the increase that is being allowed in the basic pay, I do not propose to revise the existing Scheme of Dearness Allowance". Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of reference in the State Govern ment 's order required the Tribunal to revise its scales of pay and dearness allowances, and there is no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the existing wage scales pertaining to different categories. [177A] 2.1 The Tribunal had given satisfactory reason for adopting a different mode and it was not considered necessary to interfere with the award of the Industrial Tribunal. [176B] 2:2 It is well settled that an illegality warranting interference under Article 136 is committed if some other method is adopted. The Court cannot lightly interfere with such findings unless there are glaring infirmities in the order or where the error has been manifest and apparent on the face of record. [175C D] 3:3 In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appel lant and decided "to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category". The Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service.
