The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents, an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2 per day, and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said Award. The appellant paid its employees only As. 10 / per day and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the authority that section 15 was applicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. Held, that even under the unamended definition of 'wages ' as defined by section2(vi), rates of remuneration prescribed by an award could not be included. In dealing with the question of construing the unamended definitions of the term "wages" it is essential to bear in mind the scope and character of the powers conferred on Industrial Tribunals when they deal with industrial disputes under the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms of contract between the parties when they dealt with industrial dispute under the , Industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms Of contract between them, and the employees. If it is shown to the satisfaction of Industrial adjudication that the terms in question need to be revised in the interests of social justice.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged under section 409 with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which was under his charge to his own residence and under section 477 A of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him under section 465 and section 409 of the Penal Code. On appeal by the State, Held, that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and there has been considerable divergence of judicial opinion on the scope of section 197 (1) Of the Code. The question whether sanction was necessary under section 196(1), will depend upon the facts of each case. If the acts complained of are so integrally connected with the duties attached, then sanction under that section would be necessary; but if there was no necessary connection between them and the performance of those duties, the official status furnishing only the occasion or opportunity for the acts, then no sanction would be required. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The State of Bombay ([1948] L.R. 75 I.A. 185), approved. Shreekskantiaah Ramaiah vs Emperor (I) L. R. 75 1. A. 180, referred to. Held further, that the sanction was required under section 198(1). There has been a considerable divergence in judicial opinion between the highest Courts in this country and by the Privy Council, and the position may now be taken to be fairly well settled. Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor ([1948) L L. J 75 I A.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. It filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore state and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful but the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that state. At the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs " and was answered in favour of the assesse. Held, that the assessee was entitled under section 30(1)(i) to deduct from the profit a loss of profits or gains under any other head in that year the losses arising under the head business were sustained in an Indian State or in the latter case in any other Indian State and so divided the loss as aforesaid could not be deducted. The words "profits" in section 10 meant business in British India or business in an I.T.R. , referred to.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the company is at Calcutta. It has Branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55. The first respondent claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the Company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the ageof 58 subject to their employee passing a Medical examination on reached the age o of 55. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that no such trend was established in fact. The age of compulsory retirement for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. The Tribunal had considered this factor and came to the conclusion that the age was not fixed at 58 or at 60 but on a closer examination it was clear that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years. Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs The Workmen, ; , applied. Dunige Band and Northern Assurance Co., Ltd. vs The workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869, explained.

The first respondent was the Chairman of a company which was formed in 1961 and to report to the Company Law Board inter alia "all the irregularities and contravention in respect of the provisions of or of any other law for the time being in force and the person or persons responsible for such irregularities and breach. " The order was made by the Chairman on behalf of the Board by virtue of the powers conferred on him by certain rules to which we shall refer later. On June 4, 1965, the Company preferred a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ directing the company Law Board and the Inspectors from giving effect to the order dated May 19, 1965 and also sought some other incidental reliefs. The order of the Chairman was challenged on the grounds that (1) the order was passed mala fide; (2) that in making the order the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(b); (3) that the order having been made by a Chairman of the Company and not by the Board; and (4) that it was made mala fide because no honest opinion was formed on the matters which under the section give rise to the power but on irrelevant and extraneous material, and further because the order of distribution of business amongst the members of the company law Board could not be done. Held:(1) The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and, therefore before they are finally known, all that is necessary for the exercise of the power is the opinion of the board that there are circumstances which suggest to it that fraud and other kinds of mismanagement mentioned in sub cls. (i) to (v) have been utilised by the company as a cloak for taking action under the provisions Of section 235. The powers can be exercised for ascertained facts and if they are disclosed by the Company, the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. In other words, the power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 (b) is merely administrative it is difficult to appreciate how the allocation of business of the Boards relating to the exercise Of such power can be anything other than a matter of procedure. For sub section (6) of section 10E provides that the Board shall, in section S5SCI 23(a), constitute a Company Law board and the Chairman may, with the previous approval of the Central Govern ment, delegate its functions to the Board and to control (1 ) (2)(a) of sub section 4A. (b).

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to two years ' rigorous imprisonment. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption in the case had not been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in their case, According to the appellant there was no other evidence in the present case which points to the complicity of the 14 appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they could be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn is one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity. HELD : The conviction of the appellants was correct in all the circumstances of the case. As regards the sentence, the offence no doubt was serious. But no injury beyond one appears to have been caused. Therefore, a sentence of three years ' imprisonment will meet the ends of justice in this case. [723 E] In the present ease the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders and they had been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. It may be 723 therefore, that the time gap in some cases is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away.) The time gap was too short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In two cases only the time period gap is about 19 days. Even then, the time lag is too long for original offender to have dispose of the properties to these appellant Or to be having left the property in their possession till suchtime as the old offenders could have taken them away.

The petitioners challenged the validity of Section 5 of the (12) of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The grounds on which the vires of the provisions is attacked are that the section gives an unguided, unchanelised and arbitrary power to the State Government to include any substance as poison for the purpose of restriction to be imposed on the posses sion for sale and sale of the same. It was further contended that the restrictions imposed on possession for sale were not reasonable restrictions. The petitioners also took the plea that though the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory treatment as it is left to each State Government, to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and regulated the decision in one State to include the substance as medicine. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The provisions of both Sections 2 and 5 of Act are not hit by any consti tutional limitation. [225A] 2.1 Section 4 of the Act impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as a poison. It states that the State Govern ment may by rule regulate the possi sion of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such poison for tho purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the possession thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which we can even take judicial notice of, that the substance known as 'thinner ' as it was or mixing with some other substances are taken as intoxicating spirit endangering the life. [226B C] 2:2 The provisions Of both Sections 3 and 5 are not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.

The appellant firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 2,68,385 written off as irrecoverable. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of the appellant 's business as chemists and druggists nor in the way of their money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income tax officer but in appeal the amount was allowed in the return of income for the assessment year 1953 54, the appellant claimed allowance for Rs. 1,68385 writtenoff as irrecoverable in the books of account as irrecoverable and that the Tribunal 's order was very brief and that it gave no reasons in support of its conclusions. The High Court held that the debts were not one incurred in the business of money lending or for any other purpose as preferred to para 7 above. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The question should have been referred in the form suggested by the appellant in their application under section 66(1) with appropriate variations. [419 D] (2) The Tribunal 'has not found the facts of the case from the evidence on record in the light of the arguments advanced at the bar. It has merely observed that charging of interest cannot make it a money lending account. [420 E] (3) The tribunal has found that the monies sent by the assessee to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of its money lending ' business, nor in respect of any other business of the assessee. This finding covers the entire amount sought to be deducted. In view of this finding which is binding on this Court, it cannot be denied that the findings reached by the Tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel, filed an application for grant of lease of the land in question. The Government of West Bengal by its letter dated September 9, 1981 addressed to the Secretary of the Zoo, the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department, suggested that the Zooo should continue to get the services and facilities in the existing structures until they were reconstructed on the adjacent land. The Minister for Metropolitan Development submitted a note to the Chief Minister pointing out that the four acres of land were agreed to be relinquished by the Committee of management of theZoological Garden on condi tion that alternate arrangements were made for shifting the existing structure which was necessary for the ZO from the plot in question to the adjacent plot. The Chief Minister sent his reply pointing out the urgency to the proposal to give the land for construction of a Five Star Hotel on the Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels. The Secretary, Animal Husbandry Department, who had expressed his opposition to the proposals to lease out the Begambari land, to the ZOOO and to lease the same to the said company. The matter was taken in appeal by the appellants before the Division Bench which held that the decision to lease was not unreasonable or arbitrary and that taking away of four acres from the Zoological Park was not detrimental to public interest. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the interests and the requirements of the zoo were totally ignored and not kept in mind when the decision was taken to lease, the land to a Taj Group. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of thezoo when they decided to grant four acres out of the eight acres of Begumbar land which was not used for the main purpose of the said zoo for the construction of five Star Hotel. [249F] 1.2 The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act, 1904 vested the Begobari land in the Managing Committee of the lordi ty of the Taj group of Hotels in regard to leasing the Hastings House property and the Begumpari land. It was on September 10, 1981 that the Cabinet finally took the decision that the lease granted to the Begamambari Land to theZoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. The Court cannot lightly assume that the action taken by the Government is unreasonable or without public interest because, as we said above, there are a large number of policy considerations which must necessarily weigh with the Govern ment in taking action and therefore the Court would not strike down governmental action as invalid on this ground unless it is clearly satisfied that the actions is unreasonable. [250F] 2.1 In view of the policy, no resin would be auctioned by the State and there would be no question of sale of resin in the open market and in this situation, it would be totally irrelevant to import the concept of market price with reference to which the adequacy of the price charged by the state to the second respondents could be judged.

The assessee, Dr. R.S. Gupta had maintained an account in the books of Messrs. Tika Ram and Sons Pvt. On 1st January 1957, the account showed a credit of Rs. 1,50,000 on 1st Janu ary, 1957, Rs. 25,000. By that letter the assessee had directed the company to debit his account to the extent of Rs 1,51,500 and credit the respective amounts in the names of the aforesaid per sons. The copies of this letter were sent to one Om Prakash Gupta and Ved Prakash Gupta. There was no dispute that instructions of the assessee were car ried out by the Company and relevant debit entries and credit en tries were made in the respective accounts. On the same day i.e. on 31st March, 1957 Om Parkash Gupta wrote to the assessee, his father, thanking him for the gift of Rs 25,00,000 made in his favour and the gift was held to be valid. The assessee contended that a total sum of Rs., 1,49,000 was validly gifted by him to his sons and grand sons by his letter dated 1st February 1957; that there was no valid gifts; that a large sum of money was validly transferred by him in favour of his sons, grand sons and hence the amounts had been wrongly included in his net wealth by the Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that the sum of RS. 1.50 lakhs was properly included in the assessee 's net wealth; that the amount of Rs 67,560/12 was rightly included in its net wealth. On reference, the High Court answered the first question in the negative and so far as the second question is concerned, it declined to answer as it did not arise in view of the answer given to the first ques tions and the questions Nos. In case of entries in the book of account by credit and debit, the sums should be available on the date of gift in the account of the firm whose accounts are said to be credited or debited; and that the amounts were wrongly included as a deduction in the net wealth of the asses see. The High Court also held that there had been no valid gift on the dates of entries, then it could not be held that subsequently, when the money was transferred by further entries in his books, it resulted in a valid gift. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that gifts were invalid as they did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.67,560; that on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal right ly held that gifts made by transfer en tries in the Books of debtor company were valid; that under section 123 of the , in case of gift of movable property, the transfer may be effected by delivery; that gift is defined in section 122 of the as transfer of certain existing mova ble or immovable property made voluntarily and without consideration by one person called the donor to another, called the donee, and accepted by or on behalf of the donee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in answering the question in favour. [127E] 1.2 In the instant case, there was nothing existing goods to be part ed. Before the Bombay High Court, in the case of Dr. Ram Gopal Raj Swarup vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, U.P., , held that a gift by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or the family or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid transfer. The Court in Controller of Estate Duty, Punjab, Haryana, and J & K., H.P. and Chandigarh vs Kamlavati, had to deal with gift by way of transfer in the accounts books.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to Government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio additional law secretary to the government of Orissa, (b) Shri B.K. Patro, Shri K.B. Patrician, District and sessions judge of Ganjam Boudh, as deputy secretary to government in law Department, member administrative tribunal and the Registrar of the Orissa High Court, in all 15 in number. All these officers are members of the Subordinate Judicial Service. Out of these, the district and Session judges were discharging purely judicial functions. In view of article 229 of the Constitution, the power to appoint the secretaries to the Government is that of the Governor. Under the Government of India Act 1935, the powers to transfer a district judge from one post to another are that of Governor though that power was always exercised in consultation with the High Court and by large on the recommendation of the High court. In order to implement this policy, the Government was reluctant. Every time the High Courts requested the government to release the three officers mentioned above for being posted as district and session judges or addl. district and district and judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other. But at that stage the High 's request to release them was rejected by the Government. The order of the Government dated October 10 1966 was challenged in a writ petition before the High COurt which allowed the same holding that those officers had no authority to hold the posts in question. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court must be held to have that right as those posts are included in the cadre of superior judicial service. [157 D] (2) The power to transfer judges presiding over courts vested with the high court under article 235 is exclusively that of a Governor though the power was never exercised in consultant with the Chief Justice. [158 E F] State of West Bengal vs Nripendra Nath Bagchi, ; , followed. (3) The cadre with which we are concerned in this case consists of three parts i.e., (1 ) presiding officers of district courts, (2 ) the Registrar and (3), the judicial officers working in the secretariat. No doubt all these officers belong to the judicial service of the State and they were before 1962 presiding over district courts or Courts subordinate to them and as such were under the control of the high Court. [159 E F; 160 A B] (4) The question of law considered in that decision was as regards the scope of the expression "control over district court" in article 235. On this topic, it is necessary to ascertain the law bearing on the subject. As seen earlier, the cadre consists of two parts i., (i) presiding officers and (ii) the Registrar, High Court; (iii) the District and Sessions Judge of Ganjam Division, as superintendent and Legal remembrancer are included In the cadre.

The appellant, a co sharer, was born in the State of Haryana. Persons in whom right of pre empt vests in respect of sales of agricultural land and village immovable property shall vest (a) where the sale is by a sole onwer First, in the son or daughter or son 's son or s daughter 's sons or s/o the vendor; (b) if the sale was by such female in her brother or s son 'S or s.5(1) of such female after inheritance, the right of preemption shall vest: (i) if a sale is of land or property to which she has succeeded through her father or brother 's brothers or sons of the vendor or vendors; (ii) if, the sale being by such male in her sister 's brother ' s son or S.5 (1) in the mother 's 's father 's broth er 's family sons of a vendor or s tiled from his lather, the rights of preempt shall vest; (iii) if any, who are agnates, in order of succession; thirdly, in persons not included under firstly or secondly above, in Order of succession, who but for such sale would be entitled to inherit the land or Property sold and fourthly, in case the person ses described in sub clause (a), i.e., in persons who but, for such sales would be enti tled to inherit, the property or property sold and thirdly,in the co sharers jointly or severally. It will be noticed that priority for the exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the case of those falling within the same class, the exercise Of right was regulated by the use of the expression 'in order of inheritance '. The appellant, therefore, sought to exercise the right conferred on him by that provision. The courts below rejected this contention solely on the ground that it cannot stand after the pronouncement of this Court in the cases of Anant Ram vs B. Baijnath Singh ; , ; and Atma Ram vs State of Punjab & Ors., ; , referred to. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right of Pre ememption conferred in a tenant was sustained on the grounds that (i). the sale of agricultural lands and village immoveable property by a single co sharor and not by all of the co coparceners jointly, the remaining part of section 15(2) as ultra vires the Constitution; (II) the right to pre em ployed in relation to Article 19(1), (f) even if they happen to be co sharors jointly, only the other co shar ers and the tenants can exercise the rights conferred by that provi sions.

The respondent, a Hindu widow adopted one K.V Seshiah. The first wife of the respondent filed a suit for title and injunction. In the compromise deed it was recited that the petitioner had given to the second and third respondents (the two sons) an amount of Rs. 1 lakh each and the second respondent have received the same. The alienees have, however, been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Admittedly, the transfers are pendente lite. In fact if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No. 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in favour of the alienees to Seshiaah within one month therefrom. The alienation was for about a purported consideration of Rs, 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs., 1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of RS.77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The respondent No 2, however filed an application under Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the compromise decree. The trial court dismissed the application. In appeal, the High Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the Court. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 A similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 where the power of the court under Order23, Rule3 of the Civil Procedure Code in the face of an objection of one of the parties to the compromise was considered. [541B] 1.2 The alienee has admittedly been in Possession of the properties from the dates of the sale which is much more than 3 years old. Admittedly the transfers were pendente lite and, therefore, the transferees have become owners of the Property and had even maintained that there have been improvements of the land by the alienors. [543C] 1:3 The alienes have made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the agreement and it is not disposed of. The factum of compromise is not in dispute. The workmen of the appellant company were dismissed from service by the Industrial Tribunal, Gujarat. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the grounds that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. It was also contended that section 99 of the Act gave wide powers to the Employees ' State Insurance Corpora tion to enhance the benefit and it was therefore the proper authority to examine the demand. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal had examined this aspect of the controversy also and held that the additional leave demanded by the workmen would be very much beyond the paying capacity of the industry. [82 D] (2) The scheme of the benefits available under the , cannot be said to cover the work men 's demands for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. Section 61 of the is not applicable for the simple reason that the benefit granted by the Tribu nal are not similar to those admissible under Act. [83 E] (3) The Scheme of the bene fit leave has been allowed in the case of glass industries by Shree Vallabha Glass Works Ltd., Vallabhyanagar, Ogale Glass Works etc. [1965] 2 L.L.J. 149; M/s.S. University Press, Baroda, and Vijay Glass Works, Bombay. Even though the Act was applicable to the workers of the Precision Bearings India Ltd., Baroda, Hindustan Brown Bovari Ltd., Oglewadi and Vijay glass Works, Ogleadi and Vijaystone Works, the benefit of sick Leave has been granted to those workmen. [86 E F] (4) The benefit of Sick leave is lost when the Act is made applicable to that region from December 14, 1969. That was obviously under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefit which the Act allowed for as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. It is apparent that the Tribunal could not be said that had erred in restoring the benefit which they were re ceiving under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into force of the , Act. The appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments.

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed against him on 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and that there was a sudden search by the police on 24th August, 1954 at the appellant 's place for alleged possession of illicit liquor. which in fact was not found but was found. Held, that the detaining authority had acted mala fide in exercising its power under section 7 of the Act in passing the order of preventive detention and there was no violation of article 22(5) of the Constitution. The order of the detention was therefore illegal. The appellant was entitled to be furnished particulars of the grounds furnished to him. Held further, that it is not possible to state affirmatively more on the question of what is vague. It must vary according to the circumstances of each case. If on reading the ground furnished it is capable of being intelligently understood and is sufficiently definite to furnish materials to enable the detained person to make a representation against the order under which he is detained, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining authorities not in any other way. It was therefore necessary to have an idea of the ground of detention as furnished. The requirement for such communication would depend on the circumstances and the nature of activities imputed to the appellant.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged with having committed acts amounting to gross misconduct under section 16(1) (a) of the . The trial officer held that the conduct of the respondent was most unbecoming of an officer and ordered administrative action to be taken under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. HELD : The words "Subject to the provision of this . , the Central Govt. may remove a man from the serv ice. Rule 14 is such a rule. It is not ultra vires. [448 B] Section 19 makes it clear that there should be rules, and subject to the provi sions of the Act and such rules, the Central government may dismiss or remove from the Service any person subject to this Act. The power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to . the provisions , it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from service under section19 of the read with r.14 of the said Army Rules 1954, a Court Martial is not necessary.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958 came into force in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat under the Act. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty. The resolution further stated that octroi duty shall be imposed on the goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule No. 1 of the Rules. On March 18, 1963, the appellant filed an appeal before the Standing Committee under section 124(5) of the Act before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Panchayat Samiti however rejected the appeal by its resolution dated September 4, 1963. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on April 6, 1964. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was intraviress (2) that the Standing committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal on merits as the appeal to the Panchayat Samitis was barred by limitation because r. 3(b) did not require the Panchayat to fix octroi limits in the resolution passed under r.3(a). HELD: The High Court has placed a wrong interpretation on r.5. [220 E] (1) Rule 5 of Fees Rules is headed "General" and apart from definitions it consists of three rules, which read as follows: "3. Every panchayat before deciding to levy a tax or fee shall observe the following procedure, namely: (a) The Panchayat shall, by resolution passed at its meeting select a taxor fee which it proposes to levy and in such resolution shall specify the rate at which it is to be levied; (b) The panchayat shall then notify to the public the proposal together with that Part of these rules which relates to that tax or fees by beat of drum in the village and by means of a notice affixed in the office of the Panchayat and, at the village chavdi or chora, specifying a date, not earlier than one month after the date of such publication, on or after which the panchayat shall take the proposal into consideration. (c) Any inhabitant of the village objecting to the levy of the tax or Fee proposed by the Panchayat may send his objection or suggestion in writing on or before the date specified in the notice, published under clause (b).

Held further, that section 12 of the does not make the contravention of the provisions. Section 12(1), which provides for the submission of the report by the Conciliation officer within 14 months but that does not affect the pendency of the proceedings and if for some reason the Conciliation ' Officer delays the submission or his action (1) ; , 739 may be reprehensible but that will not affect its interpretation to be put on section 20(2)(b) of tile Act. The respondents were engaged in gold trade, i.e., manufacturers, shroffs and dealers in gold was found carrying on business as such dealer. The Administrator issued a notice to the respondents under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for refusing permission or grant permission. The respondents challenged the validity of section 28 on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or granting permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the grounds that it suffered from the infirmity of excessive exercise of legislative powers inasmuch as the Administrator has struck down section 28 in the manner done and in its judgment at page 87 of the paper book. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [954 F] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asstt. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; , referred to. 2.1 Section 28 confers an unguided and uncanalised powers without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. Further, the section does not provide nor is any rule brought to our notice which enjoins upon the administrator to give a hearing to dealer who seeks permission under this section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, filed a suit against respondents 1 to 3 for possession of certain properties. The trial court held that the grant was a personal Inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) Article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act does not permit any distinction to be made between transfers effected by a previous manager on the basis that the property transferred belonged to the religious endowments and those made by him on the recommendations of the previous manager. [123 E] (ii) The question as to whether the properties in suit had been sold in an execution sale, and the Privy Council decision in Gnanasambanda 's case was erroneous because on the facts proved in this case, the High Court should have drawn the legal inference that the transferor had been removed more than 12 years before the suit was filed. [124 F] (iii) The fact that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of a Temple but in their individual character as owners of the said properties, shows that the transfer was effected not by the Poojars of the temple but by persons who claimed that the properties belonged to them. [125 E F] Gnanadasam Banda vs Rachaikataswami, I.L.R. , referred to. (iv) The mere fact that a person has been removed from office by other persons who are acting as de facto managers of the Temple does not make him an adverse entry in his character. [126 A B] (v) The title of the alienees in regard to the properties covered by the said sale deed was held to have conferred title on them. The possession of the vendees in respect of the properties which was the subject matter of transfer, is irrelevant for the purpose of article 134 B. [127 F G] (vi) The appellants ' case before the trial court was that Pachaikandaswamiar had resigned his position about 27 years ago, and that even if article 134B applied, limitation should be held to commence from the date when they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 1 on the date of the removal of the earlier manager who transferred the properties. [128 A B]. (vii) The High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title of Pachaukottaswamiar has not been lost by adverse possession before the suits were filed. The appellants case before it was that the question as regards whether on facts proved, an inference can be drawn that the previous Manager or trustee had been removing, is a mixed question of fact and law, and so, it thought that the plea of limitation with which the Privy council was concerned in that case was based on article 124 of the Limitation Act. [129 A B C] (viii) The plain words of article134 B do not permit such a plea to be raised.

The appellant, Ved Gupta, had been granted a licence under the Jammu and Kashmir (Cinematograph) Act, 1989 to construct a modern Cinema Hall in a plot of land which he proposed to take on lease in Gandhi Nagar, Jammu. The said licence was renewed by the District Magistrate in the name of Ved Gupta. On April 27, 1979, a suit was instituted against Ved Gupta and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the Sub Inspector of Police, Jammu (8th defendant) for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar Jammu, is the property of the firm Apsra Theatre and for a prohibitory injunction restraining defendants 1 to 7, namely, Shri Ved Gupta from interfering with the running of the Cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction against the District Magis trate (defendant 8) restraining him from interfering in any manner with the exhibition by the plaintiff of cinematograph films by the Plaintiffs of cinematographys in premises of Apsa Theatre. The suit was dismissed by the Subordinate Judge, Jammu who held that the renewal of the licence could not be made in the names of any party other than the original licensee, namely Shri Ved GUPTA, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsarara Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Government and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the High Court and Supreme Court respectively. In March 1980, the licence for the Theatre was renewed from time to time under the Act and the Rules. On July 22. 1969, a licence was issued by District Magistrate to Ved Gupta under section 3 of the Jammu & Kashmir ( Cinematograph), Act,1989 to give public exhibition of Cinematograph films at the proposed site, a detailed description of which was furnished in the plan annexed to the application. Clause 15 of the said deed provided that the site for construction of a Cinema which had been obtained on lease by Ved Gupta shall not be their personal property but shall be the property thereof of the partnership and that the permission which Ved Gupta had obtained from the Government for construction purposes of the Theatre in the said plot shall be treated as the property 'of the partnership. On June 17, 1969, Shri Om Gupta purporting to act on behalf of a partnership consisting of himself and the two persons aforementioned (as a matter of fact no partnership had been constituted at all by that date), applied to the District magistrate requesting that the names should also be included in the licence issued to Ved GUPTA. After considering the arguments advanced before him by the counsel appearing for the parties, the District Judge passed a detailed order rejecting the request of Shri Omi Gupta and declaring Shri Ved Kumar Gupta to be sole licensee authorised to run the Appsara Cinema Theatre. He filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the legality and validity of the orders passed by the subordinate courts and the appellate authority, namely the State Govt. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the order was violative of principles of natural justice inasmuch as no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order could be passed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that even though the licence had originally been issued in the year 1977, the right of operation of the license had become the property by virtue of clauses 13 and 18 of the Partnership Deed and since Ved Gupta was a sole licensee and that he alone was the licensee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the learned Single Judge that Ved Gupta who was a party to the writ Petition cannot be legally sustained and that there was no justification for interference by the Division Bench with the judgment of the learned single Judge dismissing the writ application.

The respondent entered into an agreement with the appellants, for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory was leased to them for a term of five year on the term and conditions mentioned therein. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not he evicted. The notice then went on to state that the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises, and the appellants were accordingly required not to remove the stock or raise any money on the security thereof, and to send daily reports to the Custodian. The respondent contended that section 12 applied only to properties of the evacuee and that the movables in respect of which directions were given ceased to be the property of the appellant by reason of the sale in favour of the appellants. Held, that the rights of the parties in so far as they related to the purchase by them of the Mills and the Factory was not raised in the petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The provisions of section 12 of the Administration of Evacuee Property (Amendment) Act, 1954, are intended to repel a possible contention that section 10 applied only where there was a lease, and that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". Held further, that under the circumstances the rights Of the appellants in so much as they were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and nothing in this decision should be taken as a pronouncement on those rights.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May 1976. He further held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub division officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1973. The Board of Revenue, by its order dated 5th March 1976 held that Surendrapal Singh was born on 14 3 1963 and he was only13 years of 21 age when he was the ceiling proceeding were finalised. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Sub Divi sion Officer. A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Raghubir singh that the State having not filed an appeal under section 225 of the Act and revision under Section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955, the Board could not, while hearing the revision petition filed by Raghubir Singh set aside the orders of Sub Divisional officer and the revenue appellate authority under Section 221 of the Revenue Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court also did not go into the merits of the controversy nor was it advisable to into it and it would be for the Sub Division Officer, Hanumangarh to decide it in the light of the observations of the Board. [728B] 2. Section 221 is not subject to the other provisions of Act.
