The appellant, a newspaper employee of the 1st respondent engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable. The 1st Respondent also did not send a reply to the questionnaire issued by the Tribunal nor gave any evidence before the Tribunal in respect of the matters referred to therein. However, on 15 7 1981 the Deputy Labour Commissioner wrote to the 1 st respondent asking it to file its written statements in the matter of non implementation of the Palekaran Award as the orders of the Central Govern ment made under section 12 of the Act were popularly called. The first Respondent submitted its reply in October 1981 inter alia contending that it was not running a newspaper establishment and publications published by the company were not the newspapers and as such the Perelekar Award was not applicable to it. Again on 18 11 1982 the Deputy Commissioner wrote a letter to the Manager of the Ist respondent informing him that the 1th Respondent was liable to implement the order of the State Government made on the recommendations made by Justice P.alekar, a former Judge of the Supreme Court, as the member of each of the two Tribunals to make recommendations in respect thereof. However on 15 11 1982, the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner, Nagpur wrote to him asking it that the Ist Respondent was not liable to implementing the order dated the basis on the recommendation of Justice palekar Award as he was a newspaper Establishment. Immediately after the service of the notice the Ist respon dent filed a writ petition in the High Court questioning the validity of the notices served on it by the Deputy. The High Court accepted the plea of the first Respondent and declared that the law reports published by it were not newspaper within the meaning of section 2(b) of the . Aggrieved by the decision of the High court, the appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by an employer are newspapers and the employees employed by the Ist Respondent in their production or distribution of the same to publish the judgments of the Court or of the Courts as early as possible in their law reports, which are published periodically either weekly, fortnightly or monthly. They believe that faster the decisions are published in their reports, larger will be the number of subscribers. [782A] 1.2 The expression `newspaper ' is generally applied (except so far as concerns the important class of trade newspapers) to publications devoted mainly to recording current events, and `periodicals ' to magazines, reviews, and journals which, in so far they are concerned with current events at all, are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising sheets, periodicals into books and pamphlets, both into one another. [781B] 1:3 The expression 'news paper ' is not defined in section 2 (b)of the Act. The law Reports which are generally published by a newspaper are reports of recent decisions of the apex Court of India and of the high Courts in India which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. Article 141 of the Constitution provides that the laws declared by Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. Even apart from Article 141, the decisions of this Court, which is a court of record, constitute a source of law as they are the judicial precedents of the highest court of the land. Similarly the decisions in P.S.V.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February,1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it was alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. Clause 2 of the agreement recited that the licensee had agreed to use the premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it Was further submitted that the appellant would not terminate the said agreement earlier save and except on the ground of breach of any terms and conditions written therein. The licensor was entitled to terminate the agreement earlier notwithstanding the fact that the period was of the lease or sooner termination or determination thereof after deducting all the dues if any for payment of compensation. It was further stipulated that the licence would be liable to be terminated by the licensee on the licensee surrendering possession of the said property by removing himself and his belongings on the expiry of the period. The appellant 's application under section 41 of the Bombay Rent Act, for eviction against the licensor was dismissed by the Small Causes Court. Before the Judge, the respondent approached the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the special civil application on 9th December, 1975 and ordered eviction. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to him for conducting business. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A lease involves a transfer of an interest in land, Subba Rao, J. (dissenting) 1.2 The Court of Small Causes Bombay has jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case. [1062C] 1.3 In order to go back to the findings of the trial court and the High Courts, it was a licence and not a lease. In order that to get the advantage of section 15A of the Act, the occupant must be in occupation of the premises, as a licensee defined in section 5(4A) on the 1st of February 1973. If he was such a licensee, the non obstante clause of section 16A(1) give him the status and protection of a tenant in spite of there being anything to the contrary in any other law or in contract. But if he was not a licensee under a subsisting agreement on the 31st of January, 1973 then he did not get the benefit of the amended provision of the Rent Act.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of the erstwhile Dholpur state into the Matsya Union. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Indian Dholpur on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently, in June 1947, the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. This permit had been granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2, 1947. The respondent however could not export the entire quantity of 15000 maund 's for which the permit was granted; he could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chiuni before December 2. On May 15, 1949, the United State of Rajasthan became the Part B State of Rajpur on January 26, 1950. The United State Of Rajasthan in which the former State of Dholpur came to be merged in 1949 never recognised the obligations of the latter State of Sikar and as from March 18, 1948 by a Covenant entered into by 14 Rulers of Rajasthan including these who had formed the Former State ofRajasthan, the former state of Dholapur came to he included in the United States of Rajasthan through the Matsyas Union. On January 26 1950, the State of Bikaner was formed by Covenant entered between the Rulers of Raj Pramukh and Raj Pramukh. The Ruler of the new State became the successor of the Government of the corresponding Indian State as regards all property and assets and liabilities of the United state of Rajasthan in respect of the obligations arising there under or even otherwise, provided the law so made was within the competence of the State Legislature and did not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. The State of Ajmer in which it was formed was also a Part B States of Rajgarh, Dholpur and Karauli which formed the Matsy Union as from April 7, 1949. On August 15, 1947, when the new Indian State of Jaipur came into existence on January 4, 1949 it provided for the continuance of all laws till they were repealed or amended by the new state. The appellant 's case further was that though he asked the State for refund of this advance duty, the Government did not pay back the same to him. In the meantime, rapid constitutional changes took place after August 15. 1947 and by May 15 1949, a United State became formed including the Matsaya Union as on March 17, 1948. The new State of Madhya Bharat was formed in April 1949. It may be mentioned here that when this State came into operation on April 7. 1949, it provided that all the assets and liabilty of the covenanting States shall be the assets & liabilities of that new State. In March 1949, however, the appellant applied for refund and was refused refund of the proportionate export duty for the quantity of 10,427 maunds, 20 sears and 20 Seers of Chuni before January 26. On April 7th, 1949 the respondent filed suits against the State on various grounds; but the suits were resisted by the State in which he claimed that the liability of the appellant under article 295(2) of the Constitution was not fasten on the State as it emerged on January 27, 1950 and contended that in view of article 295 (2) the State was bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the original State unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The suits were contested by the respondent on various other grounds but the High Court held that the State had no jurisdiction to entertain the suits as it arose out of political changes and dismissed them.

The appellants who were running a market as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar was challenged by them on the ground that they contravened articles 14, 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. Held: (i) Under section 3 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, the State Government has to establish a market committee for every notified area and it shall be the duty of the market committee to enforce the provisions of the Act. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 18 of the , the State Govern ment made rules which provide for the manner in which the members of the Market Committees should be elected, and also for the constitution or continuance of sub committees. The first proviso to that section provides that after the establishment in such area of a market for the purchase and sale of a notified commercial crop, no licence for the sale or sale of such commercial crop shall be granted or renewed in respect of any place situated within such distance from the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State. The second proviso enables the Market Committee to exempt from the provisions Of the sub section any person who carries on the business of purchasing or selling any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by rules made under the Act, any person carrying on the trade of purchasing and selling any Commercial crop in quantity not exceeding that prescribed by Rules made under that Act. The third proviso authorises the said Committee to remove from the list of goods specified in the notification any goods specified therein which are not trade allowances. The effect of the notification was to eliminate, as far as possible, the middlemen and to give reasonable facilities for the growers of commercial crops to secure best prices for their commodities. The Act was an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crop crops. The constitution of the Committee in which there will be representatives of the traders and the buyers was a sufficient guarantee against the implementation of the provisions. It regulated the buying, and selling by the marketing committees within a reasonable radius from the Market, as prescribed by the Rules, no license is issued ; thereafter all growers will have to resort to the market for vending their goods. The result of the implementation would be to eliminate the, as much as possible the middlemanmen and others would have to incur unnecessary expenditure which they could not afford. The impugned provisions were therefore valid. (ii)The contention that the appellants had really two fundamental rights was not correct. The contentions must fail. (iii)The Act was enacted with a view to protect the growers, the producers and the purchasers of commercial commodities. It was an integral part of the scheme of the State Act to protect them from exploitation in the market established subject to the regulations and also to do business outside the prescribed area ; and that they were not prohibited from holding the market, as property, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of imprisonment to transportation for life. Held, that the conviction was not bad on the evidence as it did not record any evidence in support of the charge. The fact that the accused ran away from the scene of occurrence does not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. In the present case there was no evidence of any prior meeting and arrangement could indeed be determined from subsequent conduct as for example, by a systematic plan of campaign unfolding itself during the course of the action which could only be referable to prior concert and pre arrangement or a running away together in a body or a meeting together subsequently. But in the absence of anything specific it was not possible to convict under that section in the present ease there was evidence of no prior meeting. The mere fact that one man called on bystanders to help him kill a given individual and they, either by their words or their acts indicate their assent to him and join him in the assault. It is well established that a common intention presupposes prior concert. All persons can simultaneously attack a man and each can have the same intention, namely the intention to kill, and each could individually inflict a separate fatal blow and yet none would have the common intention required by the section because there was nothing specific about what preceded the assault (for the witnesses arrived after it bad started) and in the circumstances of this case the conviction under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and the sentence passed on them must be set aside.

The petitioner was an officiating Assistant Engineer in class II service. He was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class 117 he could not have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i) of Rule 56 (j)(i). In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the similarly placed persons had gone before the Delhi High Court challenging the orders of compulsory retirement and the Delhi high Court relying upon Tahiliani 's case gave them relief. Dismissing the writ petitions, HELD: 1.1 The ratio of the decision in Tahiliaiani 'S case is not correct and sub clause(i) is the general rule applicable to all Government servants and sub cl.(ii) carves out a class of Govern ment servants into a category and makes a special provision. [637B] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner had not attained the age of 50 years by the date of the order. Therefore, sub clause in F.R. 56(J)(i) comes to the rescue of the Government. But if he is only a temporary hand, he has no right to the post and can always be reverted to the substantive post, if any, on which he has a lien. [643C D] 1:3 The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(1) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Govern cors into two categories covered by sub clauses (i), (ii) and (iii) has a purpose behind it. If the condi tion indicated in sub clause 1 is satisfied, namely, the Government servant is in Class I or Class II service or post and he had entered into service before attaining the age Of 35 years, and has attained the said age of fifty, the further condition that he must substantively belong to the two classes of service or posts cannot be introduced into the scheme.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Masulipatam against the appellant Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960. The appellant Corporation contested the suit and pleaded that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. It was further stated that the proposal form was sent from the office at Guntur to the Divisional Office at Masulpatam. The Divisional Manager, Masulkotam Branch, denied liability on behalf of the appellant corporation on 28th January 1961. Thereafter there was correspondence between the parties between 1st February 1961 to 23rd December 1963 wherein the respondents plaintiffs had claimed the payment and the appellant had denied liability for the same. On 10th January 1964, the appellants filed a civil suit in which the respondents had claimed that there were no concluded insurance contract between them and the corporation was untenable, according to the plaintiffs. The Trial Court held that there is no concluded or valid insurance contract. The High Court also took the view that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment of the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance of proposal if the proposal was not otherwise accepted. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf the appellant that there had been no concluded contracts between the appellant and the respondent Corporation; that the Corporation had not filed any evidence of any order prohibiting other officers one step below in rank, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager to exercise the power of Divisional Manager; that even if the representation was not accepted by the Divisional Manager on the contrary he had stated that he had taken a decision to accept the proposal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The plea that the Divisional manager was the only competent authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf or of the respondent corporation. [356B] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this Case. [355F] MacGillivray & Parkington on Insurance Law, Seventh Edition p. 1267.) referred to.

The respondent filed a civil suit for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India Ltd. from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.O Tractors Export, Moscow, the second defendant. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal by the appellant, the High Court set aside that order and remanded the case to him for disposal according to law. In appeal to this Court it was contended that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order" as far as this Court is concerned determining the rights of parties within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). HELD: The order refusing to grant an interim ' injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. [707 B] In the instant case, the plaintiff 's suit as a result of the order of the High court may become infructuous as framed and the plaintiffs may have to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief, an order which is essentially an interlocutory order may be deemed final for the purposes of article 134(1) of the Constitution. [700 C] In this case, it was not contended that the order granting an interim ex parte injunction did no determine the right and obligations or obligations of parties in regard to the matters in dispute. The plaintiff ' s suit as such was a self contained proceeding and was finally disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

The petitioners, who were engaged in the processing of processed fabric, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order dated 4th November, 1988. The said writ petition was dismissed by the High Court on 4th Nov., 1988. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value and the value thereof of the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses, and that the manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses for the processing be Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs.,30 being the value as of the grey cloth cum price of the machine worked plus manifufac tion and profits and expenses; that the manufacture expenses for processing be RS.5. and that it was not necessary to include the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The price at which he is selling the goods must be the sale value of such grey cloth or fabric plus the values of the raw material and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. [346C D] 2. Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at Which the said manufacturer is selling such goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The prices at which the he is sell the goods should be the price of grey fabric plus that manufacturing profit & the manufacturing expense but not in any other prior profit or expense.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975, he was promoted as Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed to the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to be promoted but whether the Panchayat Council had the right of appointment to him to the Post of Head clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant 's appointment as a Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Acts came into force. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to he considered for promotions is a terms and condition on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti until they are absorbed in Government Service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Acting in pursuance of the provision of section 14(4) of the amending Act, the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appellant as a Clerk though, as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [737B C] 1.2 The appointment of the appel lant to the posts of Head Clerks being without the authority of law, the government was not bound to absorb him in the post as of a Head clerk.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math, Sauna temple and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was contested by the first defendant who claimed that the properties were owned by Mahant Shivshankar Yati and that the Amauli properties had passed to him under a will executed by the Mahant. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati had been not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saauna and Sarbbarakar. Both appeals were filed in the High Court. First Appeal No. 80 of 1964 was filed by Kedar Nath Chaubey @ Uma Shanker Yati against the declaration that theama were owned and possessed by Mahant Sri Shivs Shankar Yati. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the Thauli properties were purchased by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yatati in 1921 from the personal funds and inherited by him from his predecessor Shivpher Yati, and that he was entitled as Sarbarkar to all the properties recorded in the deity Mahadeo Ji or in the name of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yutti. The present appeal is directed against that part of the judgment and order of the High court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 There can be no presumption either way. All the facts and circumstances must be taken into consideration and on a balancing of the entire evidence it has to be determined whether the property can be said to belong to the math or deity or is the personal property of the Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. [663 F] 1.2 The amount from which the Amaiuli properties devolved on Uma Shankar Yanti and do not form part of their properties of the Math or of the temple, Sri Thakur, Gokarneswar Mahadeoji. In the present case it is difficult to conclude from the material before us that the total income from the properties belonging to the Mahant and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog arpan, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and the other obligations specified in the waqf deed. [665 F] Sushil Chandra Sen vs Gobind Chandra Das, ; , referred to.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh was 42 330 found entitled to quasi permanent allotments of 40 standard acres, and 5 1/4 unit of land was given quasipermanent allotment in another village named Humbran in the same district. The two villages were, however, 25 miles or so distant from each other. Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the Village Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. This application was rejected by the Assistant Custodian on August 20, 1952. The appellants then moved the Deputy Custodian General for calling up their review application and for revising the order cancelling their quasi permanent allot in the villages. The Additional Custodian dismissed the appellants ' application on the ground that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour of the appellant. On December 17, 1954, the appellants moved the Custodian General under section 10 of the , for review of the order canceling their quasipermanent allotments on the grounds that this cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban lands at all. The Deputy Custodian rejected the application on August 23, 1952 on the view that r 14(1) of evacuee Property Rules stood in force in the matter of cancellation by the order dated October 31, 1952, and that the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955 stood in that way. The appellant appealed to the Deputy Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The power conferred by section 19 of the Act is to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Therefore, they must prevail over the provisions of section 19(1). Bal Mukund vs The State of Punjab ([1954] S.C.R. 981), referred to. (ii)The power conferred on managing officers or managing corporations only and no one else could exercise the power of cancellation.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published in June, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the Written Examination were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the interview from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina t tion. On the other hand, it is contended on their behalf that when there was a mistake pointed out, there could be no justification to cancel it and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground of improperating the written parts of the ap plic examination and the only objection was limited to exclusion by a group. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking of a fresh exami cation of all ineligible candidates on that basis. [126E] 2.1 In the instant case, when no defects were pointed out regarding the written test and the main objection was restricted to exclusion, of a Group of successful candidate in the viva voce examination from the interviews, there is no justification in cancelling the re opening part of recruitment examinat tion.

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. Som Dass, the defendant contended that the Dwara at Landaeke was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of those properties of the dera as its lawfully appointed mahant; that the appellant had no right to recover possession of that property of the respondent, and that the suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant, the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass he was entitled to manage the properties of Dera. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit took place when Shiam Dass was elected as mahant of the appellant after the date of the death. [490C] (2) The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in property i.e., the subject matters of the Suit and the interest is the interest of the person who was the party to the suit, [490E F] (3) The words 'interests interest ' in the property i,e., "the subject matter" of the present suit and the interests are the interest and of the persons who were the party thereto. [448F G] (4) The appeal could be continued against the appellant on the death or for any other reason.

The petitioners, who were working as ministerial and non ministerial employees of the State Government, were retired from service on February 28, 1983. The petitioners challenged the validity of the amendments made to Fundamental Rules by the first notification dated October 29, 1979 and the amendment in 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amendment to the Fundamental Rules was beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature; that the amendments were beyond the power of the Rule making authority; that since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age of retirement from 55 to 58, they could not be amended retrospectively so as to take away rights which had accrued to them. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment made to the Rules was within the powers conferred by Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. It is well settled that the service rules can be as much amended, as they can be made, under the proviso to Article 309 and that, the power to amend these rules carries with it the power, to amend them retrospectively. [604C D] 2. The amendments made in the Fundamental Rule were beyond their powers. The rules and amendments made under the Proviso could not therefore be amended so as not to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be amended prospectively so as tO take away right which had already accrued to him. [505C D; E] 3. The State exchequer would have to find and pay Rs. 70 crores on one single day by way of retirement benefits, for which no budgetary provision was made. It would appear from these contentions that the reduction of the age from 58 to 55 in the instant case is not hit by Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. Besides, the point made by Shri Tarkunde is concluded by a Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Bishun Narain Misra vs State of Uttar Pradesh [1979] 1 SCR p. 865 that the very case, namely, Moti Ram Deka 's case on which the petitioners relied, contained the observation that the rule as to supperannuation or compulsory retirement resulting in the termination of service of a public servant did not amount to removal from service and is therefore violative of Article 311 (2) of the constitution. [599E F] 4. The Government of Uttar pradesh & Ors. vs State Of U.P. ; , referred to.

The appellants, a registered dealer in the State of Haryana, purchased raw materials inside the State without paying tax thereon. He then sold the manufactured goods to dealers who, in turn exported those goods out of India. On these facts it was claimed that the assessee was not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. The assessing authority rejected this claim and held that the sales effected by the appellants were not sales in the course of export outside India within the meaning of section 5(1)(b) of Act. In appeal, the High Court affirmed the view taken by the Assessing Authority. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessees are not charge able to tax either u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24(3). [353F] 2.1 The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under this Act" and "the purchase value of any goods on the sales of which tax is levied under this act". There can be no dispute that a tax is payable under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them the sales made to the purchases effected by them but for a claim for exemption under section 24. Explanation 6 inserted in section 2(p) read with the provisoes inserted in Section 24(1), w.e.f.

The goods in the goods passed to the buyers on shipment and were despatched by the sellers to an address outside the State of Bombay within a period of six months from the date of purchase by M/s. Daulatram Rameshwarlal, a firm registered under the Indian Partnership Act (referred to later in this judgment as "sellers ') are registered dealers under section 11 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The sellers contended that these were sales on FOB contracts and therefore they were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). Held, that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales were exempt from tax. The words " a person in section 8(b) of the Act are wide enough to include a registered dealer or anybody else. The intention of the parties that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of Imports (Control) Order, 1954, the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the time of export would therefore mean nothing more than that the property in the ' goods shall pass immediately before the ship goes beyond the territorial waters of the country or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. The object of the Legislature clearly is to secure that the declaration as regards intention of goods being despatched outside the state of Bombay should be carried out by despatch by " a registereddealer" to whom he sells the goods. If such despatch outside the territory of Bombay was by a person to whom the certifying dealer has sold the goods but who is not a registered owner, it cannot strictly be said that the declarations have been carried out. The scheme of the legislature clearly is that where the intention as declared has not been carried on purchase tax should be levied. To hold otherwise would be to make the declaration of the intention useless.

The respondent husband married the appellant wife as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. 15 The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance, it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise that the appellant declared her to be the absolute owner of the flat and various deposits in respect of the said flat made with the cooperative housing society. The appellant finding herself in financial straits and unable to maintain herself, moved the Magistrate under section 125 Cr. P.C., 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. She proceeded on the footing that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she had been a divorcee. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) section 125(4) would apply in the absence of proof that the lady was not living separately by mutual consent; (ii) Section 127(3)(b) would be applicable in the case where the affected party in such a fact situation is the neglected divorcee; and (iii) Section 128(4)(b), would apply. HELD: 1.1 The appellant 's plea that the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payment of mehar, it was section 127(4), Cr.P.C. [78F] 1.2 In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the Magistrate at the trial level. However, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. [79F] 2.1 In the ordinary course, a order for commis sion must follow the quantum with the quantum being determined by Magistrate at at the Trial level. But, what was the amount of meherhar ? Rs. 5000/ , interest from which could not keep the woman 's body and soul together for a day, even in that city where 40% of the population are reported to live on pavements, unless she was ready to sell her body and give up her soul ? The point must be clearly under stood that the scheme of the complex of provisions in Chapter IX has a social purpose. Ill used wives and desparate divorcees shall not be driven to material and moral dereliction to seek sanctuary in the streets. [80G H] 2:2 In this generous jurisdiction, a broader perception and appreciation of the facts and their bearing must govern the verdict not chopping little logic or tinkering with burden of proof. The next submission is that the absence Of mutual consent to live separately must be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come.

The Collector of Samastipur, after perusal of the order dated 25th March, 1988 passed by the Collector, cancelled the bid of the appellant. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order directing that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect of future contracts under the Collector is set aside. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the premises, that portion of the Order directing that a person be placed, in the Black list in question, cannot be sustained in law. [867C] 2.2 The last portion of order in so far as it directs black listing of the appel lant in respect thereof in respect to future contracts, cannot he sustained in Law. In the instant case, that part of the said Order directing black listing is set t aside. So far as the cancellation of the bid is concerned, that is not affected. This order will however not prevent the State Government or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for blacklisting ing the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do in accordance with law, i.e., giving the appellant due notice and an opportunity of making representation. [861D E] 3.3 In the circumstances, that portions of the aforesaid order directing black listed of the petitioner in respect Of future contracts cannot be sustain in law, because, if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order.

The property which was the subject matter of the dispute originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and a building thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953, all the co owners of the property (includ ing G.G.) sold the property to the United India Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) but was converted subsequently in 1961, into a partnership concern of G. and his four sons. The firm and its partners were compendiously referred to as 'the tenants '. The first lease deed (Ext. P 1) was dated 22.9. 1947 and related to Door No. 2 (Item No.1 in Schedule A to the plaint). This was a property comprising of an area of 4 grounds and 151 square feet with certain buildings thereon. On 20.7,65, the Life Insurance Corpora tion of India stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the said property. On 21.7 .65, it moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311 of 1965) in the court of the Rent Controller (Sri A. Varadarajan who later became a Judge of the Supreme Court) for fixation of fair rent in respect of item No. 1 as against the rent of Rs 150 p.m. fixed under the lease deed. So far as item 2 was concerned, it appears that at the time of hearing it was conceded before the Rent controller that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the lease deeds and that they had not constructed any of the premises thereupon. The Rent Controller rejected this contention on the ground that since the subject matters of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Authority had no juris diction to fix the fair rent. On appeal, the Court of Small Causes held that the Rent Authority had jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation and fixed the fair rents in respect thereof and that therefore the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Authori ty 's order in respect whereof the respondents had to fail.

The petitioner, who was a respondent in the writ petition, was given an opportunity to file his objections to the preliminary list. The High Court of Mysore held that the Writ Petition was premature as the final gradation list of officers on an integrated seniority list was still to be prepared after hearing objections. Allowing the appeal by certificate, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner had ample opportunity to do that. Hence, the principle recognised in Shankariah 's case (supra) was not applicable to such a case. [829F] 1.2 In order to establish the invalidity of the final list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. The Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. It was an opportunity for the Central Govern ment to establish Advisory Committees. [ 829F G] 1:3 In the instant case, no mala fides are alleged. [829B C] 2.1 There was not reference whatsoever to any facts of the case in the order of a few lines by which the petitioner 's petition was disposed of by the High Court on the conject ous assumption that it was governed by Shankarikhedah 'S case (c) The petitioner respondent, who is the respondent before this Court, was unrepresented, and therefore could not be heard by us. [828F] 2:2 In the circumstances of the present case, the respondents were entitled to an opportunity of making a representation with regard to the two points urged by Mr. Ashoke Sen before the final seniority list. [ 828B C; 829A] 2 :3 The combined final gradation lists dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, are ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1991 in para 174 of the Import & Exports Policy for April 1978 was made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the conditions was that the Additional licences issued to Export House would also be valid for the import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and 5 Part A and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by Appendix 1 Part B) and items which were `canalised ' could not be ruled out and it was in this light that the Court can be said to have used the words "whether canalised or otherwise" in the order dated April 18, 1985. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant/grant of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that petitioners had failed to diversify their export of 'Other products ' during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court. One other Writ Petition (filed by the petitioner in writ petition No. 460 of 1988) was dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court and the said petitioners filed an appeal before a Division Bench of the Bombay. While the said appeal and the other writ petition (filed in the Bombay, were pending in the High Courts, this Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1423 of 1984, Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, and other connected matters by order dated 4th April, 1985 wherein it was observed that there was no requirement of diversification of exports as a condition for grant or entitlement of an export House Certificate in the Import Policy for The period April 1988 to March 1991. In that order this Court laid down the following conditioned conditions: (1) The Additional licences granted to Export houses/Trading Houses prior to April 1, 1988 shall cease to be validfor import of item items of goods which appeared in Appendents 3 and 4 Part A of this Policy; (2) The additional licences issued prior to 1.4.1988 will cease to have the valid for import of Items of raw material, components, consumables and spares appearing in Appendix 6, List 8, Part A, and items available under this Policy.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which has its factory at inter alia, Visakhapatnam. It manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is also the case of appellant that the manufacture of fusel gas is complete and it is the fully manufactured fusel oils/Stirene Mendenceer which is stored at the factory gate, which is sold in bulk and delivered to the customers at the appellant 's factory. The fusel water/Slyrene Moulders manufactured according to the appel lant, is a Com pletelaly manufactured product and after complete completion of the manufacture it was stored in store tanks duly certified for this purposes. It was also the appellant that it is not necessary for the said gas cylinders lent by it to its customers could be included in the assessable value. The appellant had filed its price lists in respect of the same. In the said price lists, which were duly approved by the Asstt. Collector, the appellant had shown the value of furi ture oil/styreneMonomer manufac tured by it at the rate at which those were sold in wholesale as "naked Ex Works and in bulk". According to the appellant, the manufacture is complete, and it was the fully manufic tured fusel/Sterene M accessioner. It has also been the case that the aforesaid drums had been supplied by the buyer. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included In the assessable Value. Hence according to it, it was not necessary to consider the wider propositions canvassed by the two sides. It accordingly held that the value could not be included under the assessablevalue of the fusel on the ground that in any event under the Act and the Rules, the duty of excise is payable by the manufacturer on the manufactured goods. The said sub section does not contemplate, accord ing to the appellants, the inclusion of cost in the value in the price of the goods when the packing is supplied by a customer to a manufacturer on its own cost.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training School issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the PW 1, Venkataswamy, the canteen contractor as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. This was on the basis of a complaint made by the appellant that the food served in the canteen was substand ard. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant. The test was positive, the currency note were seized and the appellant arrested. At the trial, the prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10 .1975 itself passed orders and closed the file. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the accused had not been examined; (ii) that the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., and (iii) that even from the earliest opportunity that the currency Notes found in his possession was the money returned by PW 1; the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the prosecution and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 is rebutted and the conviction cannot therefore be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. [337F] State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; C.I. Ernden vs State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1964 SC 575; and Lohana Kantilal vs State, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1, referred to. (2) The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to ' be rebutted. [437H; 339A] State vs Mohamedubibeeb., ; C R. Erudernden v State of U.P., AIR 1954 SC 575 and Loahana Kantilal V.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india undertaking after obtaining release from government service. The petitioner retired from the service of the company on or about September 30, 1984. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the Company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement and in accordance with the company 's rules, he was required to pay compensation for the use of the premises. After the expiry of the said period of six months, the petitioner addressed a notice requesting the petitioner to vacate the flat stating that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company rules. Since the petitioner failed to vacate, the company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act 1971. The Estate officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner. The Petitioner challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the same set aside the eviction order and directed the Estate Officer to give a personal hearing to the petitioner and instead of availing that opportunity, the Petitioner moved the High court by a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the view expressed by the Single Judge following the earlier decisions of the High Courts in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Ranjan Jha & Anr., ; , and Amritlal Chaum vs Lal Kejriwal & Anr. , was to be preferred to the view contrary expressed by it of Calcutta High Court in Amrit Lal Chum 's case, that the words 'any such property ' in section 630(l)(b) relate to property specified in cl. (a) viz., property of a company wrongfully taken possession of by a present officer or employee of the Company and therefore both clauses (a), (b) qualify the words "any such thing" in cl.(b) thereof, and that both clauses are separated by the word 'or ' which must take its colour from the context in which it appears. The Court further held that since the petitioner had failed to vacating the flat, the Company initiated proceedings under the public Premises ( eviction of Unauthorised occupant) Act, 1971. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court of Calcutta in Amrit Lai Chum case did not lay down good law and was therefore right in holding that for purposes of prosecution cl.(a) of section 630 of the Act applied only to the existing officers and employees of a Company. [179E F] 2.2 The words 'Any such property" in clause (b), relate to any property of the companies as mentioned in cl., (a). Section 630 of tho Act clearly makes it an offence if an officer or servant of a public company wrongfully withholds possession of such property of that company.

The appellant was the manager of a private temple. The deity installed in the temple was a public religious endowment and it had been constructed by the founder of the Sansthan. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons who were members of the public. The Assistant Charity Commissioner held that the Sansthan was not a public trust but ordered its registration as a public Trust under the Act. On appeal, the District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner and declared the Sansthan to be a private property and not a Public Trust. In further appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court failed to consider all the material documents filed on behalf of the appellant except exhibit 35 and that the conclusion was highly erroneous being contrary to the one that had been reached by the District judge on appraisal of the entire documentary evidence. HELD: (i) The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour or of an individual as private property. [521 D] (ii) There was no evidence of any hindrance or restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the public extending over a long period.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 by the Third Income tax Officer, C 1 Ward Bombay, at and for Rs. 40,178 4 0. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer on the 10th April 1951 issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring him to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said demand. The Additional Collector attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the said premises by a warrant issued on the 24th March 1954. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February, 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 30th March, 1955. The sales proclamation was issued on 15th January, 1955 and the sale proceeds not being sufficient to satisfy the assessed tax the Additional Collector on the 7th June, 1955 issued a notice under section13 of the Act requiring the assessee to appear in person before him on the 8th July, 1955, and showcause why he be not apprehended and confine to civil prison in satisfaction Of the said certified demand. No payment having been made, the Additional collector attached the good goodwill and the tenancy rights and in the premises by warrant of attachment issued on 24th April 1954. On the 9th July 1955 an application was made by the present petitioner to the Bombay High Court under article 226 for a writ in the nature of a writ of habeas corpus for the production and release of the assessee. The High Court held that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 offended article 14 of the Constitution and dismissed the petition. Held: (i) The law was not dead because the assessment proceedings had been started and the certificate had been issued by the Income Tax Officer to the Additional District Collector of Bombay and the Additional Commissioner issued a show cause notice of demand and actually attached the properties prior to the amendment, the assessee must be governed by section 13 as it originally stood and not by it as subsequently amended. (ii) The tax demand being a Union demand there should be uniformity in the punishment to be meted out to defaulters and it could be done easily by suitably amending section 46 (2). The law is not dead. It was enacted to be treated as crystallised and to be applied by the Collectors, although the State laws for the recovery of arrears of land revenue may be materially altered by sub sequent amendment. What is necessary is that there must be a nexus between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Act under consideration.

The respondents, who were the trustees of the Port Trust Employees ' Union, made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. The General Workers Union was informed that if the demand was pressed a three shift system would be introduced. The workmen then retraced their steps and accepted a 2 hours ' variable recess but requested that it should be as near the middle of the shift as possible. The Trustees agreed to accept the hours of rest at fixed hours in the Alexandra Docks but at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks they kept it variable agreeing to fix it as near to the middle. Under this arrangement the shore crew working at the Master 's & Victoria Dock were informed that the shoreshould work for 8 hours and that there should be a variable rec tor of one hour and overtime of three hours should be paid. The respondents thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) On any single day the number of hours constituting a normal working day is 9 hours ' rest and the number Of hours of work cannot exceed 9 and together with the hours Of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. [638B] (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal Working day is achieved by pres cribing that the hours are fixed as near as the middle on the tides. The workers at the Weekly Reporter get a specified interval of one week for rest and this makes up their 9 hours which is 8 hours ' work and one hour interval for rest. They are, therefore entitled to three hours ' wages overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on any day. [643E F] (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Prince "s andation Docks with the cases of the Alex andra Dock or in respect of the Flotilla Crew. They point out that in the former there is 3 hours ' adolescent recess and in the latter there is 4 hours of overtime in the 12 hour shifts, but at a Prince 'S day it cannot go beyond 48. What has not been done by the Act or the Rules is to specify that the interval for each rest shall break up the hours or 9 hours of duty. [641F H] (iv) The workers compared the cases with the case in which the respondents relied on.

The appellant tenant let out the disputed property on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and the suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out to the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court allowed the revision petition set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the plaintiff suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, provisions of this Act will be applicable to the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the rights of parties will be governed on the basis of the date on which the suit is filed and it was urged that if on the date of commencement of the Act, i.e., October 1 1976, 10 years have elapsed even if the date when the suit for eviction was filed by the respondent the provisions of the said Act were not applicable then merely because the proceedings had been pending for all these years it could not he contended that as during the pendency of this matter in this Court 10 years had elapsed and therefore the appellant tenants will be entitled to protection under the Act. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in Section 20 and the language thereof is also significant. Bar of suit for possession of tenant except on specified grounds (1) Save as provided in sub section (2) no suit shall be instituted for the eviction of a tenant from a building, notwithstanding the determination of his tenancy by efflux of time or on the expiration of a notice to quit or in any other manner; Provided that nothing in this sub Section shall bar a suit for the ejectment of a tenants except on the specified grounds as provided under the section.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1 Shibtola Lane, Entally Calcutta) on the ground that the same were in arrears. The suit was decreed by a Munsif on March 18, 1949 after the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 had come into force and substituted a new definition of thika tenant. On March 14, 1953, the Calcutta Tradh Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952 was passed amending the definition of the thika tenants still further and introducing important changes in the Act of 1948. The effect of these provisions will be considered later on. Before the Subordinate Judge a point was taken that after the coming into force of the Act 1949, the Rent Controller alone had jurisdiction in respect of ejectment suits as the defendant appellant was a thikatenant. The learned Judge held that at the time when the appeal of the respondent was disposed of by the Subordinate judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenant Tenancy Act, 1949 and the definition Of thika tenancy in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a consideration of the provisions of the Calcutta Rent Act and Ordinance, the Subordinate Court held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the West Bengal Thika Amendment Act, 1952. The High Court on appeal by certificate granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the benefit of section 28 was available only if the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of the Ordinance; and (ii) the appellant could get no relief under the Act. HELD : (i)(a) The benefit of s.28 was available even if the suit had been filed before the Act but was riot disposed of in by that date, the landlord had to establish that he was entitled to possession because of the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in section 3. By section 2 of this Ordinance, a thafika tenant against whom proceedings for execution of the decree for eviction were pending and who had applied for relief under section 28 lost the protection of that section as a result of the Amending Act of 1953. [176 D] (b) The language of sections 4 and 5 leaves no room for doubt that after coming into operation of the , it was not open to the landlord to file a suit. Section 28 was meant to give relief to a thriika tenant in a case where a decree or an order for possession had already been made between the commencement of tho Act and of the ordinance and delivery of possession has not been given to the decree holder. [177 E] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred to. (ii)(a). The language in sections 4 & 5 leaves nothing to show that after December 1952, the respondent had to prove any of these grounds at the hearing of the suit he had to be considered whether any of those grounds was available to him. [179 F] Mahaddeol Mal Kanodia v Administrator General, West Bengal; , followed. (b). The provisions of sections 3 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the appellant landlord had not established any of his grounds for eviction mentioned in s.3 entitling him to ejectment. [180 D] Maha rededeolar Kanodia & Anr. vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; and Mahadeodal Kanamal Kanodia etc.

The appellants were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs 120 300 300 to Section Officers, and in 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that recommended by the Pay Commission. The appellants contended that their duties were equivalent to Private Secretaries of Hon 'ble Judges and have demanded the same pay scale which was given to Superintendents i.e. It was also urged that Bench Secretaries were a well recognised class that existed over the years and indeed superior to Section officers. The respondents contended that it offends the constitutional principle of equal pay for equal work. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Pay Commission refused to equate Benches with Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It is found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two posts cannot be said to be equal. Keeping in view the fact that vacancies in Upper Division/Lower Division Assistants are filled up by promotion from Routine Grade Assistants, it is clear that this is a second promotion for those who come directly from Lower Division Assistants and a third promotion for these persons who are promoted first to Upper Division Assistant and then a Bench Secretary. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [297C D] 1.2 The Pay Report does not support the claim of the appellants that it violates the constitutional guarantee of equal wages for equal pay work. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the State Govern ment has granted uniform pay scale and of Rs 1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Secretaries with effect from January 1, 1986. [298E F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant company was a Government Company incorporated under the , the entire share capital being owned by it. The respondent No. 1, the Special Area Development Authority for Korba Special Area, was constituted under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam (23 of 1973). The Act was passed by the Madhya pradesh Legislature in order to make provision for planning and development of land; to make better provision for the preparation of development plans and zoning plans with a view to ensuring that town planning schemes are made in a proper manner and their execution is made effective. The appellant company, which was incorporated under it, entered into an agreement with the respondent No 1 Company under which the Company agreed to contribute a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs annually to the "seed capital" of the Authority in consideration of the authority agreeing not to exercise its power of taxation or of levying any other charges on the assets and activities of the company under the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1961. The agreement provided that the property tax levied under sub section (1) shall not be leviable in respect of the following properties namely: 10(a) building and lands owned by or vesting in the Union Government; On June 24, 1976, respondent 1 made a further demand of Rs 11 lakhs on the grounds, principally, that no tax was leviable on its property since the Company was owned wholly by the Government of India and that respondent No 2 was estopped from levying the property Tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The first contention of the appellant company is that respondent I can exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Corporation or the Municipal Council had under the M.P. Municipalities Act 1956, or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act 1961, as these Acts stood on 12 February 27, 1976 when clause (d) was inserted in its present form in section 69 of the Act of 1973. The second contention of respondent is that since the appellant companies are wholly owned by the State Government, the lands 16 and buildings owned by them cannot be subjected to property tax. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The lands and buildings on which respondent 1 has imposed the property taxes cannot be regarded as the property of the Central Government for several other purposes like attachment and sale, there is no reason why, for taxing purposes, the property can be treated as belonging to that Government as distinct from the company which has a juristic personality. [15E F] 1.2 The lands & buildings onwhich respondent 1 had imposed the tax cannot be said to belong to the Madhya Bihar State Government and were taken on lease for a period of 30 years by the appellant Companies. [16F G] 2.1 In order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that Act and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their jurisdiction. [17F] 2:2 The property tax is imposed by respondent 1 under section 127A of the Municipalities Act and section 135 of the Municipal corporation Act. This position is made clear out of abundant caution, by clause (4) of section 133 of the MP. Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 which provides that nothing contained in section 133 shall apply to the tax mentioned in clause (a) of sub section(1) of Section 132, which shall be charged and levied in accordance with section 135. The third contention of Attorney General flows from the provisions of Article 285(1), 286(2) and 135 of Madhya Pradesh Municipal CorporationAct, 1956.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in Venkatagiri. On January 10, 1942, an agreement was entered into between the Rajah of Venkatagiri and one Sri Balumuri Nageswara Rao whereby the Raja agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate quarry within his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942 if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by the lessee during the preceding year. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Raja to him. No notice was issued to the manager of the estate requiring him to take over possession of the slate mines and other ancillary reliefs. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945 and that as the lease was for a period exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal by the State, Held, that the notice dated December 27 was not invalid on the ground that it did not give three months ' notice to the lessee or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. The notice dated January 13, 1951, fell under the second Proviso and was valid. A. M.S. vs State of Madras, ; , referred to. Held further, that on a true construction of the provisions of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, it could be held that the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order dated December 26, 1955 was bad as it did neither give three month ' notice nor provide for compensation as contemplated by section 299 of the Government of India Act. A person who came into power later declared its intention to abolish all zemindaries and intermediary interest in land must be held to have committed an overt act to terminate the transaction.
